This edition of our photography prompt series wants your subjects jumping into or out of the frame. It's summertime, the possibilities come alive, and we can't help but let that reflect in our images. A dip in the pool, submerged or floating calmly on seawater, chaotic underwater snapshots – we want to see those. Here's to preserving our summer memories in the best, most vibrant light! To share them with us, use the tag #intheframe and #intothewater.

Credits: jaapjan, sugarcottonlamb, hobbylinse, cjaehnl & ale2000

Many of us have those memories – poised on the edge of a precipice, eyes set on the vast expanse of water below. We count to three and jump; there's no thrill like diving deep. Alternatively, we find quiet in between the wind and water, floating aimlessly, thinking about nothing and feeling everything. This edition of In the Frame wants to see those moments, the calm and excitement of diving into or wading through water.

Some photos just scream excitement, and we want our Community members to answer these questions: what makes these photos special? Is it the angle, the shifted colors, the specific instance captured on film?

Credits: reinermao, theprime, juditpanxeta, justopenit & fetish230

Views from the High Ground

Thank you to our Community members who've submitted their shots for the From the High Ground edition of our series! We always love seeing the world through your eyes. From action shots to street scenes, here's a small gallery featuring submissions from the Community.

Credits: locutus, koentraire, raffaele\_rossi, joecool & rishona

We’re excited to see your photos! Share them with us by using the tags #intheframe and #intothewater. To explore submissions from the Community, visit #intheframe.

For Bird, the photographer behind Film Full Photo, shooting on film is more than about documenting a moment; it's a way of telling stories through the photographer's own eye and emotions. She used the Lomomatic 110 to bring her Solo Wedding concept to life, a personal project she created to share the idea that “Happiness doesn't depend on someone else – it begins with ourselves.”

Every frame captured with this tiny camera not only preserves a meaningful moment, but also reflects her unique creative vision and heartfelt approach to storytelling. If you're looking for inspiration for your next shoot, read on and discover Bird's beautiful images captured with the Lomomatic 110. 💍👰🏻

Solo Wedding Project by Film Full Photo

Welcome to the Magazine, Bird! How did you first get into photography, and what was your first camera?

My journey began when I was in vocational school studying design. Photography was offered as an elective, and that's where I first picked up a Nikon FM2. Developing and printing photos in the darkroom with my classmates was a lot of fun, but at the time I wasn't especially drawn to photography, because my dream back then was to become an interior designer, so I was much more interested in drawing perspectives and painting with watercolors. Still, the Nikon FM2 was the very first camera I ever used, and it marked the beginning of my analogue journey.

Credits: Film Full Photo \| Shot with the Lomomatic 110 & Tiger 110 ISO 200 \| Model: @cartuneishappyverygoodgirl

What was your first impression of the Lomomatic 110?

“How can something this cute exist?”

That was honestly my first thought when I saw it and held it in my hands. Even the film cartridge looked adorable. Everything about it felt playful and reminded me of LEGO toys from when I was a kid. I have to admit that the first roll was a bit challenging because I wasn't used to zone focusing. But by the second and third rolls, I was having so much fun. I found that shooting this way let me react much more quickly and capture the exact moments I wanted.

Credits: Film Full Photo \| Shot with the Lomomatic 110 & Tiger 110 ISO 200 \| Model: @cartuneishappyverygoodgirl

Please tell us about your concept for this shoot.

Solo Wedding started as a fun personal idea inspired by a photography trend in Japan, where many women choose to wear wedding dresses and have bridal portraits taken without a groom. To me, it represents the joy and freedom of living life on your own terms. Whether you're in a relationship or not, whether you choose to get married or not, you can still wear a beautiful wedding dress and celebrate yourself through photography.

I started this project by photographing myself wearing a wedding dress. I wore a vintage dress from my own shop and captured a series of self-portraits in front of the dressing room mirror.

Solo Wedding Project by Film Full Photo

In your photos with the Lomomatic 110, the bride is seen enjoying the beach on her own without a groom. Can you expound on the particular message you wanted to convey?

I've noticed that whenever people see beautiful pre-wedding photos, many women leave comments like, “I wish I could do a photoshoot like this, but I don't have a boyfriend,” or “If I ever get married, I have to shoot with this photographer.”

That made me wonder, what if you didn't have to wait for someone else to be there? What if you could simply do it for yourself? That question became the starting point of this project. I decided to turn the idea into reality, and in the end, I truly loved how it turned out.

Credits: Film Full Photo \| Shot with the Lomomatic 110 & Tiger 110 ISO 200 \| Model: @cartuneishappyverygoodgirl

Why did you choose the beach as the backdrop for this shoot?

Our model, Toon, has a playful personality and is someone who loves being active. I wanted to incorporate something that genuinely reflected who she is, so blending her interests into the shoot felt like the right approach. The location – Tal Sam Ton Beach in Pranburi – has a beautiful coastline and a long road running alongside the beach, making it the perfect setting. One of my favorite moments was watching Toon effortlessly hop onto her surf skate and ride along the shore. That image has really stayed with me, it was such a charming moment and matched the seaside atmosphere perfectly.

Credits: Film Full Photo \| Shot with the Lomomatic 110 & Tiger 110 ISO 200 \| Model: @cartuneishappyverygoodgirl

As someone who has photographed many pre-wedding shoots, do you have any tips for helping couples feel relaxed and natural in front of the camera?

I think it all starts with understanding who the couple really is – their personalities, interests, and what makes them feel comfortable. When people are free to be themselves, everything naturally falls into place. Pair that with a relaxed, friendly atmosphere on set, and the photos will reflect genuine emotions without feeling forced.

Credits: Film Full Photo \| Shot with the Lomomatic 110 & Tiger 110 ISO 200 \| Model: @cartuneishappyverygoodgirl

Besides the Lomomatic 110, I noticed that you also use other Lomography cameras. What made you choose Lomography, and do you think they're different from other film cameras?

I also own a Sprocket Rocket, mainly because I love the exposed sprocket holes. I've always been a fan of that look, it instantly gives photos a true analogue feel. Another favorite is the LomoKino, which I've recently started incorporating into my vintage-style video projects. It adds a playful touch and brings a classic film atmosphere into the footage.

For me, Lomography cameras have a unique charm. They add personality and help complete the feeling I'm trying to create in my work.

Credits: Film Full Photo \| Shot with the Lomomatic 110 & Tiger 110 ISO 200 \| Model: @cartuneishappyverygoodgirl

Has shooting film with Lomography cameras changed the way you think about photography?

I think cameras are a bit like people. Some days you want to be serious, and other days you just want to have fun. The camera I choose depends on the mood I'm trying to create, because each one has its own unique character. Lomography, in particular, adds a fresh perspective to my work. It brings color, character, and a sense of fun to the creative process.

Credits: Film Full Photo \| Shot with the Lomomatic 110 & Tiger 110 ISO 200 \| Model: @cartuneishappyverygoodgirl

If you had to choose the best time of day to shoot a pre-wedding session on film, what would it be?

Film works beautifully at almost any time of day. For pre-wedding shoots, though, I always prioritize what works best for the couple. Most people prefer to sleep in and arrive well-rested, so I usually plan the session for the afternoon and continue shooting through sunset and into twilight. That gives us beautiful light while keeping the experience relaxed and enjoyable.

Credits: Film Full Photo \| Shot with the Lomomatic 110 & Lobster Redscale 110 ISO 200 \| Model: @cartuneishappyverygoodgirl

If you had to choose just one of the 10 Golden Rules of Lomography, which one best represents you?

I like several of them, but if I had to choose just one, it would be Rule #1: Take your camera everywhere you go. Whether I'm working or simply enjoying a day off, I always feel better with a camera by my side. Every moment is unique, and once it's gone, you can never go back and capture it again.

Finally, is there anything you'd like to share about your upcoming projects?

I'd love for everyone to keep following the Solo Wedding project. I'll continue developing it with new themes and concepts so that each series feels fresh and different. I hope you'll look forward to the next set of images. Thank you so much!

A big thank you to Bird for sharing her story with us. If you'd like to explore her unique perspective on film photography or follow the ongoing Solo Wedding project, be sure to visit her Facebook and Instagram pages for more of her work.

We recently handed the new Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor to film shutterbug Tree, inviting her to document her travels across Thailand. The half‑frame format gave her room to shoot freely – sunrise on Koh Samet, street corners in Bangkok; all those fleeting, unplanned scenes. After her trip, we talked about the journey, the camera, and how film keeps memories fresh.

Photo by Tree \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

Hey Tree, welcome back to Lomography Magazine! You took the new Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor with you to Thailand. How did the shooting go overall? Any unforgettable or funny moments you'd like to share with our readers?

Shooting this roll felt light and easy.

With a non-half‑frame camera, I tend to be more careful about when I press the shutter – I’d hesitate, wondering if a scene is worth the frame, or if I should save it for something else. But the half‑frame camera kind of sets you free. Double the shots, half the hesitation. It gives you this liberating sense that you can afford to waste a few. So this roll ended up full of light, casual clicks that I wouldn't normally have taken.

The highlight was definitely on Koh Samet, watching the sunrise and then just wandering along the beach, sitting, spacing out, watching the waves roll in. I took a lot of photos that morning, pointing the camera wherever the sunlight hit: up at the sky, down at the rocks, random directions. At the time, I thought maybe I was overdoing it, but when the film came back, I was glad I did. Each frame carried the warmth of that moment, like being pulled back to the beach, with the light shimmering on the water and the sound of the tide still in my ears.

Photos by Tree \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

You're no stranger to LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200, and you've shot half-frame cameras before, too. So, with these two coming together this time, did they end up surprising you in any unexpected ways?

The colors of LomoChrome Classicolor are never too loud. They carry a certain cinematic quality, leaning warm and subdued. When paired with the half‑frame format this time, the zone‑focus lens seemed to make the grain more pronounced, giving the images a rough texture, almost like the grain of a fading memory.

With Thailand’s intense sunlight and vivid surroundings, did the colors and atmosphere captured on film match the Thailand you remember?

It does, though perhaps a little softer than my memory.

In my mind, Thailand is vivid – bright, saturated, with that relentless tropical sunlight. But film tends to pull that intensity back slightly. Seeing the scans, I appreciated that distance. It didn’t amplify the heat; instead, it preserved the dampness of the sea breeze, the glare of the streets, with a touch of the dreamlike. For me, film doesn’t just record color. It holds onto the sensory texture of a moment as well.

Photos by Tree \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

How did you find it as a travel companion, or as a camera you could simply pick up and take with you?

I really enjoyed keeping it in my bag and taking it out whenever I felt like it. It's light and easy to carry; you never hesitate to reach for it, and you don't miss a moment just because pulling out the camera feels like a bother. It also has this distinctive shape, a bit like a small flask, unusual and cool in its own way. On trips, I find myself drawn more and more to those unplanned moments, and this camera just fits that rhythm.

Photos by Tree \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

With 72 shots per regular roll, you don't have to reload as often. Did that change the way you approached your shooting rhythm or your mindset while photographing?

The biggest difference? It gave me the confidence to “waste” frames.

Half-frame is basically a money‑saver. With a half‑frame camera, I found myself taking more photos with no particular purpose – shadows while walking, power lines and flowers when looking up, a passing cat curling up for a pat, or just a patch of light falling across a surface. When I went through the scans, I realized those were the ones I liked most – the unplanned moments that, pieced together, ended up forming the real memory of the trip.

Photos by Tree \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

If you had to pick one favorite photo from this trip, which one would it be? And what makes it special?

I’d pick the one where a friend and I arranged fallen frangipani flowers into a heart shape.

It was the last day in Thailand. We’d just been wandering through a park when we passed a frangipani tree with petals scattered all over the ground. We gathered them up and shaped them into a heart. Just as we were about to leave, the sun slipped out from behind the clouds, so we each picked up one more flower and captured the moment. Looking at that frame now, it still brings back that small, quiet happiness. A single image, holding the memory of a feeling.

Photo by Tree \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

Who would you say this camera suits best?

I’d say it’s ideal for anyone new to film. It’s a point‑and‑shoot – easy to pick up with no steep learning curve, yet it gives you a genuine taste of the joy of documenting life on film. It’s also great for travelers, or anyone who already enjoys capturing everyday moments. If you tend to shoot sparingly, the half‑frame format might just encourage you to press the shutter a little more often. Some of my favorite shots have come from moments I didn’t plan, and I’ve grown to appreciate the unscripted ones the most.

Photos by Tree \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

Finally, do you have any advice for those planning a trip and hesitating about whether to bring a film camera along?

If there’s still a little room in your bag, bring a half‑frame camera along.

Film has a way of stretching out the joy of a trip; it keeps the memories fresh. When you get your scans back weeks later, a single frame can bring back a moment you may have already forgotten pressing the shutter for, something that might have felt entirely ordinary at the time.

Photos by Tree \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

Thank you to Tree for testing the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera and sharing her travel experience with us! Follow her RED to keep up with her analogue adventures. Curious what travel memories this camera could bring back for you? Try the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera and let it preserve those light, unscripted moments along the way.

Rebeca Morimoto is a bit like a real-life Hannah Montana, living a double life as an illustrator and a tattoo artist. Yet, that split doesn't fully capture the depth of her creative persona. Bold colors, groovy characters, and an emotional sensibility drive her creations, which recently made their way onto the La Sardina Camera & Flash DIY. In this interview, Rebeca reflects on how the analogue medium brings her back to the grit of artistic creation, keeping her excited for new techniques to discover.

Customized La Sardina Camera & Flash DIY by Rebeca Morimoto

Hi Rebeca, and a warm welcome to Lomography Magazine! Please introduce yourself to our Community and tell us what role analogue techniques play in your work.

Hi there! Thank you so much for this opportunity. I actually used to be a Lomography user back in my university days, around 2012, and admired your \[movement\] so much. Collaborating with you more than 10 years after feels like a dream!

My name is Rebeca Morimoto. I’m a Peruvian Japanese illustrator and tattoo artist currently living in Australia. My artistic journey started with analogue techniques. Before I got my iPad, I used to experiment with different mediums, from acrylics to ink, and from linocut to watercolor.

When I bought my first iPad, everything changed. It became so easy to create, erase, and edit my illustrations that I slowly lost confidence in my analogue skills. I've been trying to reconnect with them for a while now, but it's taken longer than I expected.

All the recent advances in technology and AI have encouraged me more than ever to return to analogue techniques. Drawing with pencils and markers brings me so much joy and freedom. I now appreciate every imperfect line and all the uncertainty that comes with creating something by hand.

© Rebeca Morimoto \| Shot with La Sardina Camera & Flash DIY & LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed 35 mm ISO 400

What inspires you to create, and what do you love creating the most?

I draw inspiration from my emotions and the world around me. Trying to understand myself through drawing has been a form of therapy for years. I draw the things I want to remember and share: thoughts, feelings, little moments, and ideas about holding on to joy, faith, community, and justice in this world.

I try to balance justice with tenderness, and sensitivity with strength. I guess that's simply a reflection of how I see myself: strong and soft at the same time.

Please walk us through your custom La Sardina DIY project. Where did the design idea come from?

I'm a tattoo artist, so I wanted a camera covered in tattoos. I usually tattoo flowers, skulls, and birds, so they naturally became my main source of inspiration. I wanted to look at the camera and immediately recognize myself in it.

I was honestly too scared to paint the whole camera and accidentally ruin it! So, I decided to combine analogue and digital techniques instead: I painted some parts by hand and created the main illustrations digitally. That balance between analogue and digital has become a big part of my artistic language.

Customized La Sardina Camera & Flash DIY by Rebeca Morimoto

From the initial idea and through the creation process to putting La Sardina to use, which was your favorite part of this project?

Definitely experimenting with double exposure! It was my first time ever trying it, so I watched a bunch of tutorials and read lots of Lomography articles to learn how to use it properly. I wasn't even sure I was doing it right, so seeing the final results was such a surprise. I completely fell in love with them, especially when I combined double exposures with the flash. It was such a fun experience!

© Rebeca Morimoto \| Shot with La Sardina Camera & Flash DIY & LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed 35 mm ISO 400

Tell us about a day you documented with your custom La Sardina. What was the experience like, and what was it like to shoot with your very own unique camera?

I used it for the first time during my partner's birthday. We invited some friends over, and it was so much fun taking photos of them. Especially because I want to keep memories of friends we’ve made so far in this new country. Everyone was excited about the camera, and it made me so happy to share it with them.

I also took the camera for a walk along the Yarra River in Melbourne and captured some of my favorite views in my favorite spots. Living in this city has made me want to shoot more analogue photography than ever before.

Do you have any exciting upcoming projects, some creations we can look forward to?

Here are some of my tattoos and late illustrations!

© Rebeca Morimoto & tattch.tattoo

You can follow me through my two Instagram accounts: @ rebeca.morimoto for illustrations and @ tattch.tattoo for tattoos (sometimes I feel like Hannah Montana, living two different creative lives with two different versions of myself!). Thank you so much again for this opportunity. We’ll keep in touch!

Thank you, Rebeca, for bringing La Sardina to life and brightening up our day with your bold designs. Follow Rebeca on Instagram and see the creative process behind the final camera in this video.

If you want to learn about useful tips for shooting multiple exposures, visit this tipster: How to Master Multiple Exposures, and make sure to check the gallery of other creative La Sardina customizations!

When Scotland played in the World Cup, the Tartan Army marched and cheered their way through the streets of Boston, drinking the bars dry, crowning local statues with traffic cones, and forging lifelong friendships with bemused locals. Glasgow-based videographers Ralph McClure and Keir Reid of Clubhouse Paradiso were two of the thirty thousand Scots who made the journey to the USA.

Armed with the ActionSampler, they captured the chaos on film, later stitching the frames together into a series of short animations that bring the trip’s vibrant energy and atmosphere to life. We caught up with Ralph and Keir to discuss the creative process behind this project.

Photos by Ralph and Keir of Clubhouse Paradiso \| Shot with the ActionSampler

Hello, Clubhouse Paradiso! Please tell us a bit about yourself.

Hi! We’re Ralph McClure and Keir Reid, the founders of Clubhouse Paradiso, a creative studio based in Glasgow. We specialize in videography and photography, creating work for clients across a range of industries, including hospitality, sport, and the food and beverage sector. We met while studying at the Glasgow School of Art and launched Clubhouse Paradiso shortly after graduating.

What made you want to try the ActionSampler camera?

We were looking for something a bit different to document our trip to the World Cup.

Photos by Ralph and Keir of Clubhouse Paradiso \| Shot with the ActionSampler

Tell us about these photos. Where did you take them, and what did you shoot?

We traveled to Boston to follow Scotland’s World Cup campaign while producing a travel vlog for our client, Open Goal. We spent our time filming across the city, capturing the atmosphere around Boston as well as the action at Scotland’s opening match against Haiti. The ActionSampler was the perfect companion for the trip. Its compact size made it easy to carry throughout the day, allowing us to capture dynamic stills in between filming without slowing down our workflow.

You turned these into some stop-frame animations. Explain that process and how you found the results?

The developed film split each exposure into four photos. We separated these into four layers in Photoshop, stacked them on top of one another, and saved each as a .psd file. We then dropped the file into Premiere Pro and created a sequence that played each still photograph in succession. This meant we could duplicate the sequence many times, creating an animated stop-motion loop.

Sound plays a big role in our work, and we try to create original music tracks and sound effects to complement our visuals. This really brought the looping animations to life! We loved blending these analogue and digital techniques together to create something unique.

Photos by Ralph and Keir of Clubhouse Paradiso \| Shot with the ActionSampler

What song would you each choose to reflect the ActionSampler?

The first thing that came to mind for us both was something textural and grainy.

Keir: Hopeless - Shlohmo

Ralph: Leaves - Nicolas Jaar

Photos by Ralph and Keir of Clubhouse Paradiso \| Shot with the ActionSampler

What's coming up next for you guys?

Alongside our regular client work, we’re looking forward to shooting a couple of exciting campaign films for projects that are still under wraps. We really enjoyed using the ActionSampler, and the response to the work has been amazing. We’re excited to keep experimenting with more Lomography products and seeing where they can take our work next!

To see more work by Clubhouse Paradiso, visit their Instagram page and website.

For this photo shoot, our LomoAmigo Riccardo Montanini tested the LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200 Film through two different visual styles: one softer and dreamier, and the other more vibrant and rich in color. He also used the Petzval Art Lens to give the portraits a more dreamlike quality, creating a series of images that demonstrate the film's versatility in different contexts and lighting conditions. In this interview, he talks about his experience of the shoot and the creative process behind it.

© Riccardo Montanini with the Petzval Art Lens and the LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200

Hi, Riccardo, welcome back to the Magazine! Would you like to tell us about your day with the LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200? Where did you take it and what did you shoot?

Hi! To try out this new film, I spent a day shooting with my friends Anna Haholkina and Marcella Apollonia. Ginevra Di Cesare, our stylist, joined us to help us choose our outfits. We shot around Milan’s Bicocca neighborhood and in Monza Park, trying to make the most of one of spring’s first sunny days, and also to maximize the potential of this film’s low ISO 200 speed.

I used my reliable Nikon F100 camera with these lenses: a 35 mm AF F2, a 50 mm AI F1.4, and a Petzval Art Lens to accentuate the dreamy look we wanted to achieve. For the photos featuring the leaf wreaths, I used a combination of filters to alter the film’s native look and achieve a distinctive color palette: a low-contrast 1 + 1 or 2 Kodak Color Wratten CC30B filter stacked on top of another. However, for the photos featuring more colorful outfits, I left the film in its original state, without making any alterations.

© Riccardo Montanini with the Petzval Art Lens and the LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200

What were your initial thoughts when you saw the results? How would you describe the mood created by the film?

It’s definitely a fine-grained film comparable to Color Plus or Color Negative 100. It has fairly warm, reddish undertones that faithfully reproduce skin tones with a natural look. However, since we were never in direct sunlight, we only used it in low-contrast situations, so I can’t say I’ve really pushed its dynamic range to the limit. In my opinion, its characteristics could really shine in a summer setting under the sun, whether in portrait or landscape photography. Overall, I would say that it's a versatile film with a pleasing look and less extreme shifts than other emulsions in the LomoChrome series.

© Riccardo Montanini with the LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200

Which aspect of the color rendering impressed you more: the contrast or the grain?

The Classicolor 200 has excellent color rendering. Though it has not been tested to the extreme, it maintains a good curve width without being too high-contrast. It features extended and detailed midtones. I also like how the primary colors are captured. Reds and yellows stand out particularly well without appearing unrealistic or exaggerated. I’ve also noticed a blue-green undertone in the shadows that can make the image look even more distinctive. The grain is present but not excessive, similar to other 200 ISO films. It responds well to filters and maintains a realistic appearance, even with some adjustments.

© Riccardo Montanini with the Petzval Art Lens and the LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200

Do you have a favorite photo? If so, what makes it special to you?

I see this roll of film as having two main sets: one with flower crowns and one with brightly colored dresses. The best shot in the first set is probably the close-up of Anna holding flowers out toward the camera. With her intense gaze, dress, and flower crown, combined with the low-contrast look and Petzval lens that guide the eye to her face, I’d say it’s the perfect embodiment of our vision for this set.

For the second set, I’m divided between two photos: the one of Marcella adjusting her glasses while lying on a towel in the middle of the lawn, and a close-up of two girls with different expressions without their glasses. Both of them work well from multiple perspectives and reflect the intended look and mood of this set.

© Riccardo Montanini with the Petzval Art Lens and the LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200

What song would be the perfect soundtrack for this roll of film?

Since I've significantly altered the natural look of this film, my perception of it may be distorted. For the first half, I’d say something like Teardrop by Massive Attack works well, while Let It Happen by Tame Impala might be a good fit for the second half, with its natural colors.

© Riccardo Montanini with the Petzval Art Lens and the LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200

What situations or projects would you like to use this film for in the future?

I used it for portraits this time, but I’ll use the next roll for something different, like a photo essay on one of my business trips this month or a summer vacation. It could work well in places like the Cinque Terre or the mountains. In any case, I hope to shoot on a sunny day to test its dynamic range.

© Riccardo Montanini with the Petzval Art Lens and the LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200

What advice would you give to other photographers who want to try out the LomoChrome Classicolor Film for the first time?

It's probably a good film for beginners, someone looking for that vintage aesthetic and classic vibe, maybe while on vacation. I used it in a completely different context, and I have to say it works just as well that way. However, unless you’re always carrying a tripod with you, this film definitely needs plenty of light and should be shot during the day, unlike some other films that can handle low-light situations.

Thank you, Riccardo, for sharing your photos and first impressions of the LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200 with us! To see more of Riccardo's work, visit his Instagram page.

After the success of our first LomoApparat LomoWalk with art and craft supplies store London Graphic Centre in 2025, we returned to do it all again in 2026! For this walk, we used the LomoApparat, and each participant was able to choose between Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400, LomoChrome Metropolis ISO 100–400, or LomoChrome Purple ISO 100-400 film for the day. They were also shown how to use the Close-Up, Kaleidoscope, and Splitzer accessories.

In this article, we talk to London Graphics Centre Marketing Executive Vivika Chugh and participant Elisa Giust, and share some of the results from the LomoWalk.

Photos by Hannah Brown

Welcome to the Magazine! Please tell us about London Graphic Centre and why you think analogue photography is so popular.

London Graphic Centre is a space for artists, stationery lovers, makers, and hobbyists. It's been an important part of London's creative community for decades, evolving from an art store into a destination for art, stationery, craft, and hobbies. We're always looking for innovative and exciting products, so there's always something new to discover in store.

I think analogue photography has become so popular because people are looking to move away from screens and engage with something more tactile and creative. It encourages you to slow down and be more intentional with what you're capturing. Film also creates colors, textures, and effects that feel unique and organic in a way that digital photography can't replicate.

Photos by Pallavi Bhatta with the LomoChrome Purple ISO 100-400 & Dolly with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 \| Shot with the LomoApparat

How did you find the walks and the results from the LomoApparat?

I found the walk a really great way to engage with the camera and with London. Even though I work in central London and walk around the area all the time, I noticed so many things I wouldn't normally pay attention to because I was actively looking for subjects to photograph. The results were so different from what I would get from my phone, which made the experience even more exciting. I loved the colors and textures of the film photos, and it was really fun getting to experiment with the different lenses and effects. It definitely made me want to shoot more film.

Photos by Silvia Pizzini with the LomoApparat & LomoChrome Metropolis ISO 100–400

Talking about the day, participant Elisa Giust says:

> “We decided to sign up for the walk to try something new. I love photography, and I had already used a film camera before, but not a point-and-shoot as an adult (I did use disposable Kodak cameras when I was a kid), and I was curious to try one. James came along out of curiosity and enjoyed the walk so much that he decided to continue experimenting with film cameras in his free time. It was quite fun to just take pictures without thinking about aperture, shutter speed, etc.”

Photos by Elisa Giust using the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 & James with the LomoChrome Purple ISO 100-400 \| Shot with the LomoApparat

> “James enjoyed the whole experience, meeting other people and capturing London with a film camera (something he hadn’t done before). We thought the results were quite fun, and it's always exciting to get the photos back, whatever the results. Some of the photos came out better than we could've imagined; others gave us a good laugh. All in all, a great experience!”

Brimming with all the colors of the spectrum, members of the LGBTQ+ community from around the world join in a global celebration of Pride Month every June; and with its roots centered on advocacy, equality, and empowerment, Pride has always culminated with a march in commemoration of the Stonewall riots of June 28, 1969.

This year, Lomography staff from across the globe attended Pride parades organized by their respective local communities. Capturing with them scenes of solidarity was the new Half-Frame Simple Use Camera, pre-loaded with LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200.

Photos by: Antonia Klengel, Min-Seon Choi & Syd Watts with the Half-Frame Simple Use Camera

Through the eyes of Miriam Duarte, Antonia Klengel, and Wiktoria Kowalczykova, we were given a backdrop of the Vienna Pride Parade. With intimate close-ups and colorful candids, their series of diptychs visually encapsulates just a few of the hundreds of thousands of attendees who flooded the Vienna Ringstrasse in a sea of love and unanimity.

Photos by: Miriam Duarte, Antonia Klengel & Wiktoria Kowalczykova with the Half-Frame Simple Use Camera

Taking us through the streets of Namdaemun-ro and Ujeongguk-ro was Min-Seon Choi with snapshots from the Seoul Queer Culture Festival held in Korea. Min-Seon’s side-by-side frames tell the stories of a community’s call for better visibility and representation.

Photos by: Min-Seon Choi with the Half-Frame Simple Use Camera

Lastly, Syd Watts takes us to the NYC Pride March in Manhattan. Syd uses half-frames to highlight placards with calls for radical inclusion, and equips the camera’s flash and gel filters to document moments with friends from the march in lowlight.

Photos by: Syd Watts with the Half-Frame Simple Use Camera

These few photos taken by Lomography are just part of a bigger picture that Pride is a shared experience, more than just a parade; a singularity towards a fairer and more equal society. Pride marches remain historical reminders that prejudice and discrimination have no place in a world that claims to uphold human dignity, regardless of who they choose to love.

We hope these moments we’ve shared with you inspire you to embrace self-expression and to allow yourselves a sense of unrestrained creativity. May you imbue the spirit of Pride, beyond the annual march, through both the lens and life!

Discover the story behind his latest work, where he beautifully translates the feeling of being drawn into nature by utilizing the lens’s unique swirly bokeh and immersive wide-angle perspective.

Hello! Welcome back to the Lomography Online Magazine. Could you please start with a brief self-introduction and tell us about your main areas of work?

Hello, it’s wonderful to meet you all again. I’m Jihu Kim, and I am still out here chasing and capturing dreamlike moments.

© Jihu \| Joseph Petzval 27 mm f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Art Lens \| Model: Dana

You recently tried out the Joseph Petzval 27 mm f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Art Lens. Compared to the other lenses you’ve used in the past, what was the most impressive difference?

To be honest, I was a bit worried at first because 27 mm is quite wide compared to the 35 mm or 50 mm lenses I usually rely on. I was concerned that the signature Petzval swirly bokeh effect might be too intense, making it difficult to control according to my vision. However, just like the other Bokeh Control Art Lenses with different focal lengths, it delivered a natural yet uniquely creative atmosphere. Thanks to that, the shoot was incredibly enjoyable.

© Jihu \| Joseph Petzval 27 mm f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Art Lens \| Model: Dana

Could you share your overall production process and how you approached this project with this lens?

Since my plan was to create the entire video using only this single 27 mm lens, I spent a lot of time thinking about how to position the background and the foreground. To blend harmoniously with the lens's signature swirly bokeh, I actively tried to direct scenes that captured that “feeling of being sucked into nature”, which I personally felt while being outdoors.

© Jihu \| Joseph Petzval 27 mm f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Art Lens \| Model: Dana

Were there any specific features or characteristics of the lens that you found particularly interesting, and how did they play out in the actual work?

The most interesting part was shooting tight insert cuts. Because the minimum focusing distance is so close, I could seamlessly shoot close-ups without any hesitation, despite it being a 27 mm wide-angle lens. For this project, I wanted to leverage the outdoor location to capture wide landscapes even more grandly, while catching the light hitting the subject’s hands or shoulders in a closer, more dense way. The Joseph Petzval 27 mm f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Art Lens perfectly met those needs.

What was the underlying story or message you wanted to convey through the final footage created with this lens?

I observed a character from both afar and up close in the forest, moving as if drawn by something or searching for something. Through this, I wanted to encapsulate the mystical yet pleasant atmosphere of the early summer forest – that exact sensation of being pulled into nature.

Near the end of the shoot, I happened to see Dana looking around and wandering happily. At that moment, I thought, ‘Ah, this is how I want to end it.’ I shared my idea with her, and we wrapped up the shoot beautifully with her spinning around gracefully as if dancing.

© Jihu \| Joseph Petzval 27 mm f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Art Lens \| Model: Dana

Was there a specific scene or sequence where you felt, “This was only possible because of this lens”?

There is a wide shot right in the middle of the video where I tried to capture Dana walking between massive trees. It’s my favorite shot. The moment of filming her passing between those giant trees, beautifully distorted by the swirly bokeh, is the most memorable for me. The Joseph Petzval 27 mm f/1.7 made it possible to deliver an immersive yet vast image.

What kind of environment or scene during the outdoor shoot brought out the characteristics of this lens best?

The way the light filtered through the forest trees created countless light rings (bokeh balls), making it the perfect environment to showcase the charm of this lens. In particular, the spot where we filmed the final scene was a space sheltered by a dense canopy of trees. The synergy between those glittering light spots and the lens's unique bokeh truly stood out there.

Has this experience inspired you to try any new shooting styles or genres?

I fell in love with the wide-angle perspective so much that it made me want to increase my use of wide lenses significantly. It also left me with a strong desire to capture landscapes from an even further distance.

© Jihu \| Joseph Petzval 27 mm f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Art Lens \| Model: Dana

If there is one piece of advice you’d like to give to other creators considering this lens for video work, what would it be?

For those who are used to standard focal lengths like I am, I highly encourage you not to be afraid and just dive right in. Having experienced how its distinct bokeh richly fills up a scene, I know I’ll be reaching for the Joseph Petzval 27 mm f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Art Lens again and again.

Lastly, any final words for the Lomography Community and our readers?

I will continue to create wonderful projects while exploring diverse perspectives. I hope all of you can share in those kinds of experiences with Lomography as well.

It was a pleasure exploring the new possibilities of the Joseph Petzval 27 mm f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Art Lens. We look forward to the dreamlike scenes and fresh perspectives Jihu Kim will continue to capture. You can follow his upcoming work on his YouTube Channel.

Our Magazine series, Creators in Focus, highlights experimental minds around the world who are pushing boundaries, and finding new ways to live life more analogue.

Photography doesn’t end with the click of the shutter, and American artist Lisa Brussell’s prints prove this to be true. Fascinated by the unparalleled depth of handmade prints, Lisa has spent years exploring and combining alternative printing processes – salt, gum, palladium, cyanotype, gravure, and more. In this interview, we’re getting to know Lisa and unpacking the value of slow, hands-on processes in contemporary image-making.

Credits: Lisa Brussell \| Gum over Cyanotype

Welcome to the Lomography Magazine, Lisa! Could you introduce yourself and tell us a bit about your creative background?

Growing up, my parents shared their passion for the arts with my brother and me. I took many arts and craft classes and always had an art project going. After graduating from college with a Philosophy degree, I enrolled again to study graphic design. I worked as a brand designer and art director for consumer packaging. During this time, my role behind the camera was an art director, not a photographer. I missed clicking the camera shutter myself, watching the magic as a print develops, and having full control over the images.

When and how did you first start to take an interest in working with these alternative printing processes?

In middle school, I had a good friend whose older brother was studying photography and printing in a traditional darkroom. I was fascinated by the entire process. Once I entered high school, my first elective was darkroom photography. I set up my own home darkroom and dabbled in black-and-white darkroom printing for many years. When digital photography came, I sold my enlarger and no longer had a darkroom. I continued to be interested in analogue printing because digital prints didn’t offer the depth of a handmade print.

Credits: Lisa Brussell \| From Left to Right: Gum over Palladium, Cyanotype. Gum over Gravure, Palladium

My first alternative process was making Polaroid lifts and transfers using 35 mm slides. Soon after, I discovered photopolymer gravure. I loved the tactile quality and rich tones that could be achieved. I took a couple of workshops and was convinced shooting my digital images and making my own prints would be the perfect marriage. Once I got a press, I was in heaven – or so I thought – until I started having technical problems making plates.

As a diversion, I taught myself cyanotype and gum-bichromate printing, then learned how to combine them. Combining processes offered so many possibilities using color – I was hooked. I also discovered the Facebook group “Alternative Photographic Processes”. I became consumed with learning about and experimenting with combining many alternative printing processes – including palladium, salt printing, and most recently, ferroblend.

Credits: Lisa Brussell \| Salt Print

Where do you usually find inspiration for new projects? What’s the typical process behind your work – from idea to final print?

I mostly shoot my images during travel and local hikes, and sometimes in my backyard. I don’t follow any rigid process. When I’m planning to print, I go through my images and choose one or two that spark my interest. I usually work on two images at a time. I evaluate which process or combination of processes might work best for them. Sometimes, I pick a process first and coat my paper, then I choose my images (quickly!). I try to do at least one layer of printing most days to keep a routine going. I don’t always know where a print is going. For example, I made a salt print that turned out a bit dull, so I added some gum bichromate layers, which made it feel complete. When I’m not sure where to go, I leave a print half finished and go back and add layers weeks later.

How do you usually decide what layering approach to take?

If I know I want to print in monochrome, I will print as either photopolymer gravure, palladium, or salt print. If I’m happy with the result, it’s complete. If the print feels like it needs something, I add a layer of gum or a layer of cyanotype to give it more tone or depth. When I intend to make a color print, I usually start with cyanotype or palladium to give a sharper base to register the layers. I allow the layers to evolve as they each reveal themselves. I experiment with the process and color tones as I work. These slow and often painstaking techniques lead me to become immersed in my images. This allows me to build a more nuanced interpretation of my subject as each print evolves.

Credits: Lisa Brussell \| Gum over Cyanotype over Palladium

Do you approach photography differently when shooting images that are meant specifically for printing? Tell us about your shooting style!

When I’m shooting, I don’t plan for, or think about, printing. I’m considering composition, light, or simply capturing the feeling I have at that moment. When I’m ready to print, I review my images and select the one(s) that feel right for printing that day.

Is there a particular project or image that you're especially proud of? What’s the story behind it?

I am always looking forward to working on something new and don’t find myself focusing on any one print.

As image-making becomes increasingly automated now due to the rise of AI, what do you think is the value of slow, hands-on processes like yours?

AI will surely be a part of future image-making, but hands-on processes will always be important. That is what makes us human – it’s how we connect with ourselves and with others.

Credits: Lisa Brussell \| Cyanotype over Palladium

Are there any alternative printing processes or other forms of art that you're hoping to explore in the future?

In the near future, I’d like to experiment with printing on different papers, especially translucent ones. I recently learned to back prints with metal on vellum and hope to create palladium, salt prints, and/or gravure prints using gampi and washi papers. I also want to experiment more with salt prints and the many toning possibilities. Kallitypes are also on my list. Getting back to my first crush, photopolymer gravure printing, is up there too!

Lastly, what advice would you give to photographers/artists who are interested in experimenting with printing for the first time?

Start by choosing an inexpensive and relatively easy process like cyanotype. Look at prints and study the process to see the range of possibilities. Read alternative print books and tutorials and watch YouTube videos. Follow another printer's instructions. Take a workshop. Later, modify the process to work with your own images and printing style – everyone’s environment and touch is a little different. Learn how to create and adjust your own negatives. Create many prints. Experiment a lot. Make mistakes. Take that experience, then learn another process.

Credits: Lisa Brussell \| Gravure

Analogue endures through material processes, lived rhythms, and practices that ask us to slow down. Creators in Focus follows these sensibilities beyond photography, through voices like Lisa's that keep analogue alive across disciplines.

Stay updated on Lisa's latest experiments with alternative printing by following her on Instagram. If you want to learn more about these analogue processes, head over to our School page and explore our FAQs.

Red.

The color of passion. The color of anger. The color of chaos.

Red.

A hue that is explosively expressive, salaciously sexy and ravenously revolutionary.

Red.

The source of life and death. No, not dramatic at all. ;)

A Red-Hot Investigation

I am officially coining myself the crazy color lady of Lomography because today, I am coming at you with another In Depth piece, so fiery, you will just have to read to believe.

Inspired by the colors of Lomography, I decided to spice things up a little, and choose a color that evokes more emotions than any other. If you have failed to guess what color that is until now, I am pleased to introduce the object of my inquiries, red.

Credits: sandkorn, anafaro, scarecrowindisguise, hodachrome, neja & kleeblatt

In this In Depth piece, I get into the history of the color red, from the caves to the big screen, from revolution to film rolls. A color that represents an ultimate dichotomy: a little is powerful, too much is overkill. A small fire keeps you warm, a big fire can harm you. It is a story so evocative I can barely contain my excitement. They ( and I mean, me) don’t call me the crazy color lady for nothing.

An Inquiry into History

When we seek to understand anything, even something as materially immaterial as a color, I think it's important to start at the beginning. So, everyone, I present to you, the very first cell of the universe.

Images: Lascaux painting, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons \| Lascaux 017\_, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Nah, I’m totally kidding. We start our investigation about 17,000 years ago, at around 15,000 BCE in southwestern France. One day, over their best cup of river water, some old cave bros decided to put red ochre to stone walls and create the Lascaux cave paintings. Under flickering lamps made of sandstone and a few burning torches, these French cave people, oh la la, created a mural of bulls, horses, and other animals with the color red for the first time in human history.

Images: Lacquerware-roundbox-w-children, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons \| Vermilion pigment, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Give or take 10,000 years, we find ourselves in Ancient China circa 5000-4000 BCE. Some Chinese Artisans figured out that if you grind cinnabar (a mineral composed of mercury), you could harness vermilion, a fiery pigment used to adorn ceramic and ceremonial walls. Another thousand years later, in the 4th Century BCE, Chinese alchemists synthesized vermilion artificially by heating mercury and sulfur. They created Chinese vermilion, a more accessible form of the color, which was later turned into pastes and mixed with beeswax and sesame oil, as an early form of lip balm.

Images: Mayan Art, Bonampak, 402 AD (29627732731), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons \| Cajetes, vasijas, platos del Museo Maya de Cancún4\, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons \| Dactylopius coccus (8410000864)_, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

You thought it couldn’t get any crazier? Well, think again. Indigenous communities in Mesoamerica and the Andes discovered cochineal, a brilliant, natural crimson pigment created by crushing the bodies of the female cochineal insect: a tiny soft-bodied insect which feeds on prickly pear cacti. The Incas, Mayans, and Aztecs all used this pigment in their art, buildings, and textiles. Bright red, across almost all Meso and Southern American cultures, was a status symbol, and the color that was associated with the gods, sun, and blood.

I could honestly write a whole separate article about the wildness that this little bug inspired, but I will say, after Europeans violently colonized the Americas, this color became highly, highly coveted, and many-a European inbred emperor and pirate wanted to get their hands on it. It became the Spanish Empire’s second-most valuable export after silver.

Images: 'Madonna and Child', painting by Andrea Previtali, c. 1515, El Paso Museum of Art, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons \| Portrait of a Man in a Red Cap MET DP280848\, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons \| The Red Kerchief, by Claude Monet, Cleveland Museum of Art, 1958.39_, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Creating a New Color in Painting

European painters went crazy for cochineal, as it produced one of the most brilliant shades of red, but it did come with its own caveats. The pigment it produced was very sensitive to light, and over time, the once-bright, rich reds, faded into brown. One of the most classic examples: Vincent Van Gogh’s The Bedroom. Van Gogh used cochineal to create a violet wash on the walls and doors, but the pigment has since faded. Read this article by the BBC to get glimpses of the Art Institute of Chicago’s restoration.

Images: Vincent van Gogh - De slaapkamer - Google Art Project, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons \| Van gogh bedroom impression on original color\_, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Anyway, enough talk about a man whose painting was once used to patch a hole in a chicken coop. Red was one of the earliest colors used in European painting, meant to draw attention, both in terms of precarious anger and passionate love. It could be seen painted onto the dress of a temptress or the spilled blood of an enemy.

Other than cochineal, painters used red ochre and vermilion, and some of the most vibrant pigments were derived from toxic materials. Very fitting that a color used to signify danger was actually quite hazardous to use.

Later on in the 20th Century, synthetic paints completely changed the game. Cadmium Red was first introduced commercially in 1910, and artists like Henri Matisse began using the far less toxic alternative to vermilion in their paintings.

Images: Soldier, French Revolution, from World's Smokers series (N33) for Allen & Ginter Cigarettes MET DP838645, Public domain, via Wikimedia CommonsforAllen%26GinterCigarettesMETDP838645.jpg) \| October Revolution Seychelles stamp_, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Revolution, Auspiciousness and Storytelling

When I say red, what are the first things you thought of? An apple, ladybugs, double-decker buses in London? Well, those are nice and all, but a historian would probably think differently. Red is one of the most politicized colors in recent history and has been the symbol for revolutions and wars across the globe.

The hue represents a radical duality and is meant to trigger a little something in us. From blood spilled in the French Revolution to joy and fortune in China, of course the first color that humans perceive after black and white would be one of the world’s most powerful colors.

Images: London (UK), Bus -- 2010 -- 6, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons,Bus--2010--6.jpg) \| Iceland Poppy Papaver nudicaule 'Champagne Bubbles' Orange Center, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons \| Smithsonian National Museum of American History - Dorothy Ruby Slippers (6269207855)\, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.jpg) \| Laisee, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Red falls on the longer end of the light spectrum so it is actually a biological stimulant for your eyes and raises your heart rate. I would venture to guess that this is why many filmmakers use the color in their films very selectively, for the items or people meant to serve a greater purpose in terms of storytelling.

Take some of the most well-known red objects across cinema, from Dorothy’s slippers to Darth Vader’s lightsaber. You might forget what color the scarecrow is wearing, but those red slippers, I bet, are ingrained in your mind. And of course, I think every one of us has had a dream of walking that red carpet dressed to the nines one day.

Fiery Films and Techniques

What is film without life? Without laughter? Without the beings that we capture? Film has a beautiful tangibility, an ability to capture the effervescence of life. So, of course, red has an analogue presence as well.

Credits: paper\_negs & bccbarbosa

In an earlier article, I explored the history of Infrared Film, a film that is sensitive to light beyond the visible spectrum and leaves its subjects in bright red and magenta tones. Kodak Aerochrome was one of the most famous Infrared films which was first invented for use in the military in camouflage detection, and the color red was a significant part of that – I mean it’s literally in the name. Can’t have Infrared without “red.” Haha, okay, I will stop now.

Credits: mapix & brommi

Films that ignore the color red completely (maybe because they can’t take the fire) are known as Orthochromatic films, which are only sensitive to green and blue, so, this leads to an overexposure of the sky. Reds are darkened dramatically, which gives Ortho films their signature aesthetic. In 1906, German chemist Hermann W. Vogel figured out how to extend the wavelength up to red sensitivity, which led to Panchromatic film, the better choice for shooting in black and white.

Credits: hodachrome & buckshot

Regardless of the film you use, it has a redscale base. A technique like EBS, or Exposure Both Sides, is basically just as it sounds, where you shoot the film roll and then take that same roll and load it with the opposite side facing the lens. The reds and oranges of the base will come out with EBS, which is just a crazier, more experimental way to shoot double exposure.

We also developed our very own redscale film in 2012, which works similarly to EBS, conveniently built into a film roll. Lomography Redscale XR ISO 50–200 is available in 35 mm, 110, and 120 formats, and works in any light setting to produce warm shades of red, orange, and yellow.

Credits: atria007, yerzmyey, kleeblatt, hobbylinse & fisheyemary

A Brief Acc-RED-itation

We briefly covered the history of the color red, one that has seen the depths of caves and hard-fought revolutions. The red-hot fire and desire to create, to dream, to live courageously unites us – bring us together through our passion and chaos. Prometheus must’ve known something when he stole it all those years ago.

I encourage you to explore what red means to you, and of course, don’t forget your film and camera. Be sure to check out our Colors page for more insight into the colors the Community has dancing across their frames.

He relied on the Joseph Petzval Art Lenses to craft a visual narrative that straddles cinema, memory, and introspection. We interviewed the director to find out how the project was developed, which creative choices guided its production, and how the distinctive bokeh of the Joseph Petzval Art Lenses helped create its immersive atmosphere.

Hi, Paolo, and welcome to Lomography Magazine! Could you introduce yourself to our readers?

My name is Paolo Santambrogio, and I am a fashion photographer with over twenty years of experience. From the beginning, I’ve combined photography with directing music videos and clips within the fashion and music industries. I was fortunate to start out with film and then experience the entire transition to digital and post-production.

Working in a darkroom, developing and hand-printing black-and-white film greatly enriched my approach to photography and filmmaking. My parents were passionate about photography and had a darkroom. I think my love for photography began around the age of five or six when they gave me my first point-and-shoot camera. From then on, I was always taking pictures.

© Paolo Santambrogio with the Joseph Petzval Art Lens \| Stills from Stessa Direzione by Paola Iezzi

What inspired you to turn your passion for videography into a career?

It happened very naturally. First, I was asked to create a video to support a photo shoot. Then, I was asked to shoot a music video. From there, directing became a natural extension of my work. After all, fashion photography already has a very directorial approach. You plan the shoot, choose the models and locations, and handle the details of production and storytelling. That's why I've never felt there was a big difference between preparing a photo shoot and making a video.

Of course, the language changes. A still image must convey a concept and communicate an emotion in a fraction of a second. In contrast, a video, even a short one, requires time, rhythm, music, sound, and editing to develop its narrative. Sound design and editing are precisely the aspects I’m most passionate about. Even from the perspective of lighting and cinematography, relatively little changes for me. I almost always work with natural or continuous lighting, so my set can often accommodate both photography and video.

© Paolo Santambrogio with the Joseph Petzval Art Lens \| Stills from Stessa Direzione by Paola Iezzi

What was the concept behind the music video for Paola Iezzo's Stessa Direzione, and why did you choose the Joseph Petzval Art Lenses?

We started with the song Stessa Direzione by Paola Iezzi. It's a pop song with a refined '80s sound that reflects on life. For Paola, it's the realization that her journey has come to an end. Even when you part ways with someone you love, whether they are a partner, relative or friend, you can still move forward together. It's a metaphor for the human condition that despite our different paths, we hope to always move in the same direction.

For the production, we chose Los Angeles. We shot over the course of five days across two city locations; a laundromat and a vintage arcade, as well as in Malibu, the Mojave Desert with its abandoned trailers, and several interiors at a motel, a diner, and a very iconic gas station. Our goal was to tell the story of the song through evocative moments and images with strong cinematic inspiration. The video contains several Easter eggs referencing Blade Runner, Pulp Fiction, Breaking Bad, and Scarface, but they all stemmed from the desire to convey the emotion of this moment of self-awareness: a journey within oneself visually rendered through one of the world's most evocative cities in terms of imagery, visual emotions, and human experiences.

© Paolo Santambrogio with the Joseph Petzval Art Lens \| Still from Stessa Direzione by Paola Iezzi

What were your first impressions? How would you describe the personality and visual character of these lenses?

I’m really excited about the Joseph Petzval. From a technical standpoint, they’re incredibly convenient. They’re all the same length and have focus rings that are compatible with focus motors. They’re also compact and lightweight, so they’re quick to swap out, even in extreme situations.

We shot quite a few scenes with a guerrilla-style setup, and they were useful in that sense. Visually, they produce a three-dimensional, rich image. The colors blend beautifully, with smooth tonal transitions. The roll-off is soft and cinematic, and the overall character is distinctive without feeling artificial. We often used them at full aperture, and in many cases with the bokeh control set to maximum to accentuate the swirl and make the image more mesmerizing.

© Paolo Santambrogio with the Joseph Petzval Art Lens \| Stills from Stessa Direzione by Paola Iezzi

Were there any difficulties or challenges that you faced?

From a technical standpoint, everything went smoothly for all five days. The only unexpected event was rather surreal. During a shoot in the desert, a murder occurred about two hundred meters from our location. As a result, the entire crew was questioned by the police that afternoon to see if anyone had seen or heard anything. It wasn’t exactly the easiest situation in which to continue filming, especially for the camera cars. Such things happen in Los Angeles.

As for the rest, the most complex part was the logistics. Often, we had a three-hour drive in the morning and another three-hour drive in the evening to reach the various locations. On top of that, we also had to transport a gorgeous '66 Mustang. Navigating the desert, rocky canyons, and Los Angeles' eight-lane freeways with it wasn't exactly straightforward.

© Paolo Santambrogio with the Joseph Petzval Art Lens \| Still from Stessa Direzione by Paola Iezzi

Were there any particular moments, lighting setups, scenes, or subjects where the lenses really shone?

I was pleasantly surprised by how well the lenses performed in every situation, whether in tight close-ups with pronounced bokeh or in wide shots. They performed well in both interiors with on-screen lighting and natural settings. The scenes in Malibu, with the view of El Matador Beach, were particularly interesting to me, as were those in the desert with the Joshua trees distorted at the edges of the frame, which enhanced the psychedelic feel of those places. These are legendary locations for anyone involved in photography or filmmaking. They’re among my favorite places in the world to work.

© Paolo Santambrogio with the Joseph Petzval Art Lens \| Stills from Stessa Direzione by Paola Iezzi

How did the distinctive bokeh of the Petzval Lenses contribute to the atmosphere or style of your footage?

I wanted the journey to represent not only Paola’s physical journey as she drives through Los Angeles and the desert in the Mustang, but also her inner journey into memory, recollection, and self-awareness. It's a journey that must be completed until a choice is made. In the final scene, it’s no coincidence that Paola sets off again into the desert and throws away a photo of herself as a teenager. It's from the time when she started making music with her sister and finding success. It’s a gesture of self-awareness and maturity.

The circular bokeh of the Petzval lenses helped immensely in this regard because it forced the viewer to stay within the scene. It was almost as if they were being drawn into it, or as if there was a spiral pulling them inward. I needed this sensation exactly, and I knew these lenses would greatly amplify the final effect. The aesthetic of Los Angeles and the surrounding desert is perfect for this kind of blur; it's as if those places naturally draw you in. The lenses amplified and intensified a unique sensation for me.

© Paolo Santambrogio with the Joseph Petzval Art Lens \| Stills from Stessa Direzione by Paola Iezzi

Given its increasing presence in the world of photography and videography, artificial intelligence is a particularly relevant topic today. Do you think AI can support creativity, or does it risk compromising the authenticity of artistic projects?

I’ve always been a nerd and a geek. I love technology and new things. When digital technology first came along, I embraced it right away. For my most important portrait and advertising projects, I personally handle color grading, post-production, and retouching. Therefore, by nature, I’m very open to technological innovations. At the same time, I often shoot on film and improvise on set, sometimes in an unorganized and less technical way, setting aside the more rational and analytical side of my work. I believe my perspective on AI stems from this balance.

I don't think AI should be considered a form of creative intelligence, partly because it isn't. It merely reproduces patterns by copying and remixing human experiences. AI robs us of our creative power without adding anything interesting on its own. Unfortunately, there’s currently a lot of hype among clients who think they can save on production costs while achieving the same result. But that’s not the case. There's a risk of producing increasingly standardized images that lack storytelling, emotion, and the truth, mistakes, and serendipity that only real-life experience can generate.

If anyone can “shoot” in Brazil, Patagonia, or anywhere else on the planet with any type of model (using one, ten, or fifty models per shoot) how will brands differentiate themselves? How will they add value to their identity? I don’t think it’s a coincidence that many important photo shoots are once again being done on film. That added value is necessary to give a brand or magazine significance, positioning, and uniqueness. Another key point is this: if future photographers and filmmakers only work with AI, where will they find inspiration? Traveling for work is very different from traveling on vacation. If photographers and filmmakers don't travel, visit places, interact with other professionals and people from other countries, or truly experience their work firsthand, how can new ideas emerge?

We need regulation now, not in a few months or years. People need clear disclaimers on generated images to understand what is real and what isn’t. Perhaps we'll also need an AI tax to redistribute, at least in part, the income that creative professionals will lose and are already losing. AI is a tool and must remain so. It cannot replace anything; it can only add to, facilitate, and accelerate certain processes, just as digital photography and post-production have done in the past. However, it cannot replace the experience, eye, set, mistakes, presence, journey, and soul of those who truly create.

© Paolo Santambrogio with the Joseph Petzval Art Lens \| Still from Stessa Direzione by Paola Iezzi

Lastly, do you have any future projects that you would like to share with our Community?

Yes, I’ll be heading back to the deserts of Arizona and Utah in America soon for another project. Then, I’ll return to Los Angeles, one of my go-to places whenever I need inspiration and to recharge creatively. I’ll have more work trips in the fall, possibly to Northern Europe, and I’ll definitely be using the Petzval lenses for new fashion projects.

Thank you, Paolo, for sharing your work with us! To see more of his projects, visit his Instagram page and don't forget to listen to Paola Iezzi's new song Stessa Direzione.
