In this interview, Polish photographer and Youtuber Mateusz Zimnoch reflects on his experience with the Lomo MC-A. He shares how the point-and-shoot brought him back to the nostalgic past and reveals his preference for self-developing and scanning film.

© Mateusz Zimnoch \| Shot on Lomo MC-A

Mateusz, welcome to Lomography Magazine! We're thrilled to have you here. So, tell us – where did it all begin for you with film photography?

I got my first camera from my uncle when I was a kid. It was an old Zenit 11 with a Helios 44-M lens. Those cameras were very popular in communist Poland, and I think even today you can still find quite a few Zenits in old boxes in people’s attics or in their parents’ basements. I still have that Zenit, although I haven’t used it in a very long time. It was great that, as a kid, I could get anything at all to learn on, but as you know, those cameras aren’t exactly the best. Sometimes the film would tear halfway through the roll, the viewfinder is terrible...but that’s the camera I learned on: how to work with light, what shutter speed and aperture are.

What’s interesting, though, is that years later – when I was already working professionally in photography and video – I rediscovered that Helios lens. Today I have four of them, because every copy renders a little differently. I especially like one of them, which is unusually sharp in the center of the frame and has quite a strong swirly bokeh. I often use it for video when I can really go wild aesthetically. And in general, I have a lot of sentiment for photographic equipment from that era.

You recently got to try our latest Lomo MC-A camera. Did you have any expectations for the camera before shooting?

I had the chance to shoot quite a lot with the original Lomo LC-A. It’s an important camera, because that’s where Lomography really began – so when, years later, you released the Lomo MC-A, what interested me most was how it would compare with the original. It has an incredibly interesting lens, very unusual. A 32 mm focal length, very strong vignetting, specific color shifts, high contrast.

Most cameras make fairly similar images, but there are some that you recognize immediately. The Lomo LC-A is one of them. I think the Smena 8M is also very distinctive. There are certain specific traits in that optics that we can pick up on intuitively. And that’s what really interested me: whether it would be possible to recreate that character I remembered.

© Mateusz Zimnoch \| Shot on Lomo MC-A

So, did it work?

Definitely! You know, it’s a very strange-looking image – one you either love or hate. I really like it, especially on black-and-white films. And when you sent me the scans of my photos, in a few cases I had the impression that the images genuinely looked as if they come from the old LC-A. Especially one photo of an older woman at a train station in Romania – that one came closest to the mood I remember from the time when I was shooting with the Lomo LC-A every day.

© Mateusz Zimnoch \| Shot on Lomo MC-A

Which of the camera’s features did you come to enjoy the most throughout this process?

The three most important ones are manual mode, autofocus, and the built-in flash. These are the things that really change the way you shoot and expand the camera’s possibilities. Cameras with light meters as simple as the one in the Lomo often struggle in contrasty scenes, and it’s easy to ruin the exposure if you shoot in auto mode. Manual solves that problem, because you can read the light more consciously and help the camera choose the right settings.

As for autofocus, I found it especially useful for portraits. Focusing by eye at a wide aperture of f/2.8 is difficult, so that’s where the AF mode is most helpful. And a flash is something that’s always nice to have at hand!

© Mateusz Zimnoch \| Shot on Lomo MC-A

You travel a lot for your work as a photographer. Which spots do you find most inspiring to capture?

I really love photographing the Balkans, although I discovered them relatively late. Romania in particular is a very eclectic country – sometimes the frames almost push themselves in front of the lens. For me, it’s also a nostalgic experience to some extent, because many of those countries still have some qualities I remember from 1990s Poland. Bubbles in hot asphalt, curbs painted with white paint. You can still find those images in the Balkans, while in Poland they’ve mostly disappeared. For me, that’s a memory of childhood and a carefree time, holidays at my grandparents’ place, and spending whole days picking raspberries in the garden. Shooting film is, in a somewhat similar way, a return to the 1990s for me.

© Mateusz Zimnoch \| Shot on Lomo MC-A

You often scan and develop photos yourself. Why do you prefer to take control of that part of the process?

To be honest, the reason is very simple. When I get scans from a lab, I’m very rarely happy with them. If I had to translate that into the language of digital photography, it would be a bit like shooting RAW files and then sending them to someone who applies a ready-made preset.

And yet, editing photos is the moment when many important decisions are made! Many people have this belief that there is an objective look to photos shot on a given film stock, and that developing and scanning are purely technical procedures. That’s not true. Especially at the scanning stage, you can completely change the character of a photograph – and it’s worth taking advantage of that possibility.

While shooting with the Lomo MC-A, you got to test out various Lomography rolls. In general, is there a specific type of film that you enjoy experimenting with? If so, what draws you to it?

I have my favorite films for specific uses. For example, I like shooting everyday, snapshot-style photography on cheap amateur films like Kodak Gold. But when I do a studio session for a brand, I always reach for Kodak Portra 400 and Ilford HP5. Lomography films occupy quite a special place on that list – each of them is very expressive and clearly defined. The basic color films look a bit like expired film, but at the same time they are more consistent, which is great if I want very strong grain and specific colors, but don’t want to risk something going wrong. And I am an absolute fan of LomoChrome Purple!

© Mateusz Zimnoch \| Shot on Lomo MC-A

Lomo MC-A features such as autofocus, manual zone focus, manual ISO, and exposure compensation offer a lot of control. Did you find yourself carefully adjusting these or did you prefer to let the camera do its own thing?

It all depends on the situation. When I have time, when I can focus on composition and meter the light precisely, I prefer to work manually. But in everyday situations, or when I’m shooting street photography, I really like zone focusing and aperture priority mode.

© Mateusz Zimnoch \| Shot on Lomo MC-A

Photography and music go hand in hand. If you were heading out for a walk with the MC-A again, what song would you put on?

Difficult question! Recently, I’ve had the track “Moth” by Burial & Four Tet playing in my headphones. There’s something hypnotic about it, something that transports you into an alternative world. But if I had to choose something specifically for the Lomo MC-A? I think I’d happily go back to the album “Wisła Skarbów”, which features remixes of old Polish hits. It’s contemporary electronic music, but based on the music of our grandparents. A bit like your Lomo MC-A!

© Mateusz Zimnoch \| Shot on Lomo MC-A

Last but not least, do you have any upcoming photography-related projects you are excited about? Could you tell us a bit about what's coming?

Right now, we’re finishing this year’s edition of my Film Photography Sketchbook, a photozine that brings together a selection of my favorite analogue photographs from the previous year. This will already be the third edition, and it makes me incredibly happy that my photographs can live in this form. Not everything has to exist only on Instagram; it’s worth making things that someone can physically keep on a bookshelf. Photography itself lives completely differently on paper than it does on a screen. I think it’s very important to print your photos and allow them to exist in that way. They simply look different, they gain texture, and above all, paper doesn’t light them from behind the way a screen does.

And my next plans? I’m currently working on two projects. I won’t reveal one of them yet, but I can talk about the other. It’s very personal and nostalgic, and it’s about a small town where my parents are from. Time has, in a way, stood still there, and yet the place is slowly evolving, and more and more of the things I remember from childhood are disappearing. It’s the place of my endless holidays, visits to my grandparents, and aimless days spent wandering around with other boys from the neighborhood. I want to preserve a part of those memories for myself, and photography allows me to do that.

We are very happy that Mateusz found the time to chat with us. If the photos caught your attention, check out his Instagram and his review of the Lomo MC-A on Youtube.

RIKI is an authentic Taiwanese disco band that has released multiple popular songs in recent years, such as ‘Imma Taipei Beach’ and ‘It Wouldn't Be Christmas Town If You Weren't In Banqiao’. Behind these catchy songs that perfectly encapsulate the experience of living in Taipei lies one of the band’s key figures, lead singer Riki. We invited him to bring the Lomo’Instant Automat Glass to document his time traveling between music festivals in Taiwan and Japan. Through these instant photos, he shares glimpses of his daily life with us.

© RIKI \| Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> Hi, Lomography. This is RIKI, the leading voice of a Taiwanese disco band also called RIKI. I am down to capture the randomness of Taiwanese daily life and also the beauty in it. This is my first time using an instant camera, so I started by taking pictures of me having breakfast and walking on the street. I found it pretty fun. I tried to use the splitzer and close-up attachments, but I kept failing, which was really funny.

© RIKI \| Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> We’ve recently been working on performing at several festivals in Taiwan, and a tour in Japan. Thus, you can find pictures of us practicing, backstage, and when we’re in between shows.

© RIKI \| Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> The first show of our Japan tour took place in Kobe at a festival called COMING KOBE. We got the opportunity to perform there by winning a battle of the bands held by Taiwan Music Festival in Kenting this April. Therefore, I thought it would be a good idea to take the camera with us to document our time in Japan.

© RIKI \| Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> Since I was afraid the x-ray scanners at the airport might damage the instant film, I bought a box of film in Kobe. Pretty clever, right? (Nah.) Look, the pictures are so beautiful. I found that the camera and the photos it produced made every single thing in Japan look picturesque, like out of a J-drama. Maybe because the film is also made in Japan?

© RIKI \| Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> Having an instant camera when travelling is the best way to record memories, I believe. We just recorded our first show ever in Japan in this manner.

> I was very excited to get the chance of using a camera from Lomography. Over ten years ago, I believe it was in 2014, I visited Vienna. It was my very first time in Austria, so I bought a travel guide to plan things, like where to visit and where the fun stuff is at. One of the recommendations was the Lomography Embassy Shop. I didn’t really know what it was, but I still put it into my itinerary.

© RIKI \| Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> However, this was a sad story, because when we visited, the store had a day-off. This memory has been buried deep in my mind, until I saw the Lomo’Instant Automat Glass twelve years later.

© RIKI \| Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> In this digital world, analogue devices are becoming more and more artistic, and that’s the reason why I love using film to take pictures. It’s not only a way of recording, but also a piece of art. People are now re-embracing analogue aesthetics, for which I am happy. It is never too late to join the movement.

Huge thanks to Riki for sharing your photos and day-to-day with us! We look forward to seeing RIKI perform on even bigger stages and continue to share authentic Taiwanese disco with the world. Don't forget to follow Riki and the band on Instagram, and make sure to go to one of their gigs if you ever get the opportunity!

Jon Olav Stokke is a filmmaker based in London, and a recent Accidental Archivist, a custodian of a century of his family’s photographic legacy. What originated as a simple question Jon Olav posed to himself after his grandmother died, “where had all her photographs gone?”, led him to the discovery of 20,000 negatives recording an ordinarily extraordinary life across generations, cameras, film formats, and emulsions. Jon Olav embarked on a meticulous journey of putting pieces of the forgotten past together without any prior archiving experience. However accidental his endeavor might seem, this interview shows that the care and passion for preserving everyday life runs deep in his bloodline.

This in depth interview is part of our Archival series, wherein we uncover methods of analogue preservation and celebrate analogue photography history. Jon Olav’s story shows that everyone has the potential to become an accidental archivist and let stories from the past live a little longer.

From the collection of Jon Olav Stokke The Accidental Archivist \| Norway, c. 1947

Hi, Jon Olav, and welcome to Lomography Magazine! For starters, please say a few words about yourself, your relationship to photography, and your project, the Accidental Archivist.

Thank you so much for having me, and for the warm welcome. It means a lot coming from Lomography.

I'm a filmmaker from Norway, based in London. In 2009, I'd just started film school and fallen in love with 35 mm, and that's when my grandmother gave me her Olympus OM-1. It felt like she was passing the torch, and I've shot on that camera ever since. I've come to think of photography as an extension of what I've always cared about most: telling stories and holding on to memories. That said, I'd never call myself a photographer in the formal sense; a hobby analogue enthusiast, at best.

The Accidental Archivist came years later, borne out of a simple question after my grandmother passed away: where had all her photographs gone? That's what led me up into my parents' attic. But instead of finding a few of her photographs, I found my family's archive: three generations, both sides of the family, more than twenty thousand negatives that I'm still scanning and sharing as I uncover the stories behind them.

From the collection of Jon Olav Stokke The Accidental Archivist \| Discovering negatives in the attic.

We invited you to our Magazine’s Archival series because of your family’s photography legacy and your work on preserving it. Could you expand on why you consider yourself an ‘accidental’ archivist, and what led you to become one?

The truth is that I never set out to be an archivist, and I'm not sure I'd call myself one even now. If anything, I'm still learning on the job, a bit of a baptism by fire. That's really where the accidental comes from.

It started with Hi8 video tapes. I had distinct memories of a camera being present at every family gathering and holiday, always following me around. No wonder I became a filmmaker. So I went around the house gathering up my dad's and granddad's Hi8 tapes, which ran through the 90s. While I was hunting through boxes for more of them, I kept coming across old envelopes of negatives. At first, I barely registered them, but I began setting them aside and organizing as I went, and before long, I had a whole box, just photographs my parents had taken around the time my sister and I were born. Then, more than 50 tapes later, with the whole Hi8 collection finally digitized, my dad joked that I should do the negatives next, before Mum binned them. In her defense, 20,000 negatives do take up a huge amount of space, and it's no wonder so many families end up throwing theirs away.

What I had collected already was nothing compared to what I found in the attic, a place I'd not been for years. Going up there felt like walking in Indiana Jones' footsteps. Wedged between my baby toys and an old Guitar Hero were boxes and boxes of my grandparents' and great-grandfather's negatives, some of which none of us had ever seen. Not, I should say, the optimal place to store film.

At first, I only shared the photographs with relatives. What changed was showing them to friends. Watching someone light up at a photograph my grandfather took in London in 1954 made me wonder whether this might matter to people outside the family, and whether it might nudge others to look at their own negatives, no matter how big or small the pile. So much family history quietly disappears, and I think for my generation it's time to go up into the attics, the basements, the closets, so to speak, before it's gone.

From the collection of Jon Olav Stokke The Accidental Archivist \| From the left: France c. 1949; France c. 1949; Norway c. 1947

That's really why I do it out loud rather than quietly. Partly to encourage others, partly because the analogue photography community is so generous about sharing and teaching, that I wanted to learn from them, rather than learning alone. I also wanted to honor my great-grandfather and grandparents. These are their memories, their choices of what to point the camera at. I'm only putting the pieces back together and sharing small snippets of their extraordinary, ordinary lives.

What kind of collection are you working with, and what is your practical approach to managing such a vast repository?

It's around 20,000 negatives, with the bulk in medium format and 35 mm. Mostly color, though everything up to around 1960 is essentially black-and-white. The earliest goes back to roughly the 1910s, so there's over a century in there. Then there's a large body of 110 and 126 film I haven't been able to digitize yet, since my Epson doesn't have a holder for either format. That's the next phase, and I'm working out the right setup for it, ideally a digital camera and macro lens so the scans reach the resolution I want for archiving. The range of stocks is part of the fun: Kodak, Fuji, Agfa, and the odd outlier like Polaroid or Mitsubishi.

My approach has changed more times than I can count, but the current system goes something like this. The single most important piece, and the one I wish I'd started on day one, is a spreadsheet. Every roll gets a number, and I log the film type and whatever I can work out about it: the year, the location, the number of exposures. Not having it early on was probably my biggest mistake, so it's the first thing I'd tell anyone starting out.

The spreadsheet matters because the rolls are rarely complete, so a lot of the work is detective work before any scanning happens. I use it to puzzle the films back together, tracking down missing frames in other envelopes or lying loose at the bottom of a box. It's slow, but since 35 mm frames are numbered, rebuilding a roll in shooting order lets me follow the timeline and read the story the way it actually unfolded.

From the collection of Jon Olav Stokke The Accidental Archivist \| Discovering negatives in the attic.

Only then do I scan everything on an Epson Perfection V850 Pro with SilverFast 9, as raw negative TIFFs, then invert in Lightroom using Negative Lab Pro. And it's afterwards that I choose what to share, whether that's a photograph with a story behind it or one where something went wrong during development or scanning, which is often just as interesting to talk about.

Dating and cataloguing are ever-evolving. It starts in the spreadsheet and later moves into the metadata in Lightroom. The files live on a shared server with my relatives, which doubles as a way to gather their stories, and there’s a hard drive for backup. The physical negatives are placed in acid-free archival sheets and folders, all tracked by the same ID numbers, so anything can be found again. A lot of this, I owe to the photography community, and even a few museum curators, who were generous with the kind of advice you only learn from experience. The simplest tips were the ones that mattered most. Anti-static gloves, acid-free sheets, and a numbering system.

The photographs you restore either picture your relatives or were taken by them. What role does your personal, familial connection to the photographs play in the way you approach and engage with them?

It means everything, and I'm unusually lucky in this respect. My family has always documented itself. My grandfather built our family tree, more than 30,000 names, tracked back as far as he could reach, even tracking down relatives who had emigrated to Minnesota. My grandmother left a 200-page memoir. And my great-grandfather wrote letters and postcards to my mother and my uncles, describing the trips he took, which I'm now going through to marry with the photographs. So when I sit down with a roll, I'm rarely working blind. The family tree puts names to faces, the memoir lets my grandmother narrate her own life back to us, and the letters trace where my great-grandfather actually went.

From the collection of Jon Olav Stokke The Accidental Archivist \| Norway, c. late 1920s

That changes everything about how I engage with the images. I'm not just looking at a nice old photograph, I'm matching it to a story I can verify. A picnic from the late 1920s, captured a century ago, turned out to be the last one my great-great-grandfather ever went on before he passed away. In her memoirs, my grandmother even remembers who took the photograph and how. Without the family connection, that's simply a pleasant afternoon on a mountaintop. With it, it is a goodbye that nobody in the frame knew was a goodbye.

These photographs would still be worth looking at without any of that. They're moments in time long since forgotten, and there's something fascinating in that alone. But knowing exactly why someone raised a camera, and what was happening just outside the frame, is what makes this feel less like restoration and more like listening to my grandparents tell stories. I knew them as my grandparents. Now, I'm meeting them as children, as teenagers, long before they were anyone's grandparents, and getting to know them all over again. It's a lovely thing and a sad one at the same time.

From the collection of Jon Olav Stokke The Accidental Archivist \| Norway, c. late 1920s

Do you have a particular photo, or a story behind one, that you find especially captivating?

Gosh, where do I even begin. Narrowing it to one feels almost impossible. My grandmother in Leningrad in the late 80s, where every time they got back to the hotel, the phone would ring and go dead the moment they answered. They never shook the feeling of being watched. Stories like that keep surfacing. But the one that's truly stayed with me started with a photograph that looked like nothing at all.

From the collection of Jon Olav Stokke The Accidental Archivist \| Leningrad, c. 1987

It was a frame from a roll of 120 film, so underexposed you couldn't make anything out. I worked on it in Lightroom, and slowly people began to appear, until my mum recognized one of them. It was Alf, my grandfather's uncle, standing on a harbor, waving. Once I looked closely, I realized the photo had been taken from a boat. He was waving goodbye. And that sent me to the next negatives to find out where he was going.

From the collection of Jon Olav Stokke The Accidental Archivist \| Norway, c. 1949

It's only happened a few times so far, but I completely froze when I saw the images. I just stared at them. My grandfather, on my mother's side, a man who didn't like to travel, had set oﬀ by sea in 1949, at 26, only four years after the war, with his best friend, Tor. The photographs pick up in Calais, a town still in the early stages of rebuilding. There's one of my grandfather with the Tour du Guet behind him, wrapped in scaﬀolding, a whole city trying to put itself back together. From there, the trip moves to Paris. The Arc de Triomphe, shot from what must have been the middle of the road, classic cars everywhere. Tor standing beside a street painter caught mid-brushstroke. I found the exact spot, Place du Tertre, and the street has barely changed in all those years.

And then the part of the film could only hint at. My mum was going through a separate set of prints when she found photographs of my grandmother on the steps of the Sacré-Cœur, and by the fountain, the same spots my grandfather had stood in his. They had both been there, perhaps only months apart. We even started searching for my grandmother in my grandfather's frames, wondering if they'd somehow been there together and simply never told us. They hadn't.

Both from Bergen, no less, yet as the story goes, they wouldn't meet for another year or so. Those prints of my grandmother aren't even digitized yet. But restoring his negatives, I'm not just recovering a holiday. I'm watching two lives drift towards each other, years before they'd ever know it.

With some time into the project now, what have you learned about the process, and what have you seen change in the way you engage with each photograph?

In the beginning, I thought I'd just scan everything quickly and get it over with. I realized pretty fast that that was the wrong approach. The roll that stopped me was London, 1954. I remember my mum and dad gathering around my laptop, the three of us just staring at photographs from my grandparents' honeymoon. That was the moment I knew I couldn't rush this. I had to slow down.

From the collection of Jon Olav Stokke The Accidental Archivist \| London, 1954

So now I might spend a whole afternoon with a single image. When was it taken? Where? Why did someone decide this was the moment to capture? It's a rabbit hole, no doubt. Sometimes I come out the other side with even more questions. Other times I've found the whole story. It feels a bit like a treasure hunt, and I love that.

Of course, not every photograph gets a full arc, and I've made my peace with that. Often my aunt or my parents fill in the gaps; they'll know exactly when, where, and why. And sometimes we simply never find out, like why my great-grandfather took the whole family out on a boat and came back with these beautiful portraits of my great-uncle, the one who later moved to America. The not-knowing is part of it.

What I didn't expect was how much their personalities come through. Going through the diﬀerent relatives’ side by side, you start to see who these people actually were. My grandparents on my mum's side photographed occasions, holidays, weddings, friends; images meant to hold on to a memory. My dad's uncle Jon, who I'm named after, was the complete opposite. A civil engineer who was meticulous about his framing, deliberate about where everyone stood, their posture, their expressions. You can tell photography mattered to him. My grandparents on my dad's side were travelers, so theirs are full of landscapes, nature, and grand views, with the odd family snapshots tucked in among them. You end up with a kind of portrait of each of them, drawn entirely from what they chose to point a camera at.

From the collection of Jon Olav Stokke The Accidental Archivist \| Gran Canaria, c. 1970

Do you have any practical tips for anyone who would like to start preserving their own family's historical photographs?

My biggest tip is almost embarrassingly simple: just start. It doesn't matter whether you've got ten photographs or ten thousand; starting sooner rather than later can be the diﬀerence between knowing and not knowing.

I say that because I learned it the hard way. When I first realized what was in the attic, my honest reaction was anger at myself for not getting to it sooner. If my grandparents were still here, I imagine we'd be sitting around the computer with coﬀee and cake while they told me when each photo was taken and what was happening just out of frame. I could simply have asked my grandfather why a man who hated travelling got on a boat to France in 1949. That chance is gone now, and it's a genuinely sad thing to sit with. So if the people in your photographs are still alive, that's where I'd begin. Sit down with them. They'll tell you things about those images, and about themselves, that you'd never find any other way. Unless they wrote a 200-page memoir.

From the collection of Jon Olav Stokke The Accidental Archivist \| Self-portrait of uncle Jon

Beyond that, honestly, the technical side comes to you as you go. You don't need the perfect scanner or a system worked out in advance. Lomography's own DigitaLIZA kits, for instance, lets you scan formats like 110 with just your phone, which is perfect for anyone who simply wants shareable copies of their memories. For a hundred-year archive you might one day want to print or exhibit, you'll eventually want higher-resolution scans from a camera or a dedicated scanner, but that can come later. Start with a handful of images, see how it feels, and let it grow from there.

And, I'd add one gentle note. Not everyone is ready to go through the past all at once. Going through a lifetime of someone's memories can be a lot, so there's no shame in going at your own pace. The important part is just to begin.

From the collection of Jon Olav Stokke The Accidental Archivist \| Discovering negatives in the attic.

In the age of digital photography, what have you learned about the way people documented reality at times when only analogue media were available?

Scarcity, more than anything. Developing film was expensive, even back then, so having gone through as many analogue photographs as I have, what strikes me most is that my relatives would take a single photograph of a moment they wanted to keep. It made the act intentional. You rarely see the same frame twice. You might get another image from the same afternoon, but it's always a diﬀerent view, a diﬀerent angle. One photograph of the crowd, not 40. One of the view, and on you go.

Compare that to now, where a single family photo means firing oﬀ 50 shots in burst mode and hoping that somewhere in there everyone kept their eyes open. And then we keep the other 49 too, which is how we all end up with tens of thousands of images on our phones we'll never look at again. There's something else in that, though. When you only take one frame, you leave room for accidents, and accidents are often where the magic is. The double exposure, a strange bit of light leak, someone glancing the wrong way. The deliberate digital version tends to tidy those away. We've even started painting people out of our photos now, because it's become so easy, when back then the strangers in the background were often the most interesting part. I've grown rather fond of the strangers in the archive.

So, I don't think that what we photograph has really changed. We still take pictures to hold onto moments. What's changed is the sheer volume: 50 versions of the same pose, and I think that can make the result feel a little more constructed and a little less genuine.

And then there's the simple fact that analogue is a physical thing. Stored properly, and not in a damp attic, a negative can sit in a box for a hundred years and still scan beautifully, which is the entire reason this project is even possible. Meanwhile, we've all had the hard drive fail, or realized too late that we never backed something up, and just like that, it's gone for good. Trust me, I've been there, and it isn't fun. There's a real irony in it. The fragile-seeming old medium has lasted, and the eﬀortless new one might be the easier one to lose.

From the collection of Jon Olav Stokke The Accidental Archivist \| From the left: Gran Canaria, c. 1970; Grandma's Flowers, c. 1970

What do you wish for your project’s future, and is there going to be a point when you consider it finished?

When I first started, the answer was easy. I'd consider it finished once every negative has been digitized. But the further in I get, the more that line keeps moving. Sharing the journey with the photography community has put ideas in my head I can't quite shake.

If I could one day honor my relatives with an exhibition somewhere, I think that would be the most beautiful ending I could give this. A few people have urged me towards making a photography book, too, and I haven't let myself think about it too seriously yet, partly because it depends on what's still waiting in the roughly 18,000 negatives I haven't scanned. There could be anything in there.

So, in honesty, I'm not sure it's ever really finished. The scanning will end eventually, but by then it won't feel like the point anymore. It started as a way to rescue some old film, and it's become a way of keeping my relatives, and the world they photographed, alive a little longer. I can't quite see myself wanting to close the lid on that yet.

Thank you, Jon Olav, for sharing your story with us. If, just like us, you find The Accidental Archivist inspiring, go and experience more of his compelling storytelling on Instagram @ accidental.archivist and YouTube.

If you are a lucky owner of historical and old family photographs, share their stories with us at [analoguearchive@lomography.com](mailto:analoguearchive@lomography.com).

Hi, Lomographer! If you're reading this, you more than most likely have heard of, or have in your hands, the new kid on the Lomo block – the Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera, which combines the ease and pocketability of a Simple Use Reloadable Camera with the double duty firepower of half-frame photography.

This camera (and YOU!) are capable of telling the most fun and unique stories, so in this tutorial, we're catching you up on how to reload the 35 mm half frame camera. Let's also talk about tips you can consider for making the most out of this nifty wonder.

How to Reload the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera

Step 1: Rewind the film

When the Film Advance Wheel cannot advance and you can't press the shutter anymore, the film is finished. Turn the Rewind Knob clockwise to rewind the film until you feel it loosen.

Step 2: Open the film door

If it's your first time reloading after the preloaded film, take out the stickers on both sides of the camera. Then, press the sides of your Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera and open the film door. You can now remove the film. This should also reset your Film Counter to “0”.

Step 3: Insert new film

Slide your fresh (or expired!) film into the Film Chamber on the left-hand side of the camera.

Step 4: Secure the film onto the Taking Spool

Gently flatten your film and make sure it matches the Sprocket Wheel in the middle of the Camera Chamber. Then, hook the first perforation on the tip of the film into the Taking Spool tooth in the right-hand side of the camera. Pro-tip: turn the Advance Wheel a little to ensure your new film is hooked onto the Taking Spool.

Step 5: Close the Camera Back and turn the Film Advance Wheel

Once your new film feels snug, gently close the Camera Back. Lastly, turn the Film Advance Wheel, and press the shutter button until your Film Counter shows “1”. And that's it!

How to Use the Flash and Colored Gel Fresh Filters

Step 1: Select a Colored Gel Filter

Slide the filter of your choice onto the Flash. Use one filter at a time, or mix and match multiple colors to experiment with exciting colored flash effects!

Step 2: Turn on and charge the Flash

Press the Flash button once. The Flash Indicator will light up orange. Once the light stays bright, the flash is fully charged and ready to go!

Credits: Jacinta Luo, Tony Sotelo, Jane Fan & Rodrigo Toledo with the Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera

Making the Most Out of the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera

Now that you know how to reload your 35 mm reloadable camera, you might be wondering how to maximize this handy little half-frame. We've gladly taken the camera out for an initial spin, and here are some of the many ways we've enjoyed it, which you might enjoy, too!

Diving into Diptych Stories

You saw it coming! Diptychs are a classic with half-frame cameras, and the freedom to unfold a narrative is one of the most exciting things to do with the Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera. From capturing chaotic scenes in a parking lot and hard launching a new hairstyle, to seeing patterns in nature and documenting spontaneous bursts of child-like happiness, this camera has been the best companion for telling stories through two frames.

Credits: Rodrigo Toledo, Werapat Nenbumroong, Lomography Manila & Chloe Fuller with the Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera

Getting Closer & Catching the Craziest Moments

Do it wacky, or do it with a story. The 35 mm half-frame camera's 0.6 m to infinity fixed focus makes this a great camera for close-up portraits in style. Shoot it indoors with the built-in flash, experiment with angles, or simply fire away to catch the craziest of moments during a hangout. As we always remind you, don't think, just shoot!

Credits: Oto Zlamets & Naruporn Thawornthaweewong with the Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera

On a beach trip, in the snow, during a morning walk or an afternoon run, with two seconds or 20 minutes to spare, to click the shutter fast or linger in the scene a little longer. Whether it's to have fun or to look for tiny bits of inspiration, glimmer or glitter, the Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera is built for every moment outside the box and under the sun.

Credits: Tony Sotelo, Lomography Manila & Rodrigo Toledo with the Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera

Early in 2026, the analogueNOW festival offered a wide range of activities for photography enthusiasts, including exhibitions, artist talks, and meetups, as well as practical courses on experimental photography techniques. As part of a double exposure workshop, Lomography was delighted to be part of the festival by providing cameras and film. We were particularly happy to hear that Laetitia Heisler ( @laetitiaheisler), who’s already been a guest in the Lomography Magazine, led the workshop.

In this article, Laetitia tells us where her artistic practice has taken her since our last interview, what continues to inspire her creativity, and which projects are coming up in the future. Festival co-organizer Freia Fahrenholtz also joins to reveal the story behind analogueNOW and the workshop. To wrap it up, workshop participants weigh in with their own reviews and key takeaways.

Photo by Valentina Fernandez ( @valenfernandez)

Hi, Freia! Please introduce yourself: who are you, and what’s the story behind the analogueNOW festival?

Freia: My name is Freia and, as of this year, I am a member of the organizing team for the analogueNOW festival for analogue photography. Founded in 2013 by Sabine Alex, analogueNOW is a low-threshold, non-profit festival for analogue and experimental photography, which now takes place annually in Berlin.

The festival is supported and organized by the non-profit association click e.V. Its goal is to bring together artists, photographers, curators, educators, and photography enthusiasts to promote analogue photography. As a collaborative collective, analogueNOW organizes a diverse range of events throughout the year. The program focuses on three main areas: firstly, supporting emerging and established artists working with analogue photography through exhibitions, artist talks, and Show & Tell events. Secondly, introducing a broad audience to analogue photography through workshops for teenagers and adults, ranging from beginners to advanced amateurs. And lastly, networking Berlin's analogue photography scene – including photo labs, artist collectives, and institutions – as well as building international partnerships.

Photos 1–2: Stefan \| Photo 3: Valentina Fernandez ( @valenfernandez)

Hi, Laetitia, good to see you again! Could you also introduce yourself to our new readers? What have you been up to since our last interview?

Laetitia: I’m Laetitia Heisler, a visual artist focusing mainly on analogue photography. I’m originally from France but live in Berlin. I've been travelling a lot as usual, going back and forth between the darkroom for stills in Edinburgh, where I enlarged many of my double exposures on paper, and my current residency at Künstlerhaus Otte 1. There, I’m working on a project that transforms instant images and RA-4-prints into tangible material. Through this process, the photographs leave their two-dimensionality to become three-dimensional, taking over physical space.

How did the workshop for double exposures come about?

Freia: I met Laetitia Heisler while she was showing her work during one of our Show & Tell events in January 2026 at the Sonderfilmlab in Leipzig. When finding out that she also offers workshops about double exposures, it became clear that we really wanted Laetitia to be part of our festival.

Laetitia: I started doing double exposure workshops three years ago in Hamburg at Khrome. I love sharing this skill and teaching others a new approach towards analogue photography. I’m really interested in the temporality between two exposures by exposing the same film twice.

Photos 1–3: Nina d'Hostel ( @ninouhda) \| Photo 4: Stefan

Freia: The request to Lomography came from the wish to involve Lomography as a sponsoring and networking partner due to its long-established, strong presence in the world of analogue photography. Your experimental and low-threshold approach, as well as the joy of simply “trying stuff out,” perfectly fit the concept of our festival. After we sent our initial inquiry and had a face-to-face meeting in Vienna, we were really happy to receive sponsorship in the form of cameras and films. We're hoping that we can continue this cooperation in the future!

Was there a moment during the workshop that particularly surprised or touched you?

Laetitia: I love it when participants start connecting, taking pictures of each other and just having fun. In moments like these, the process becomes more important than the final result. It’s also one of the reasons why I use analogue double exposures in my practice: This process creates an antidote to our overly efficient and digital world.

During the workshop, you shot with LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100-400 and LomoChrome Turquoise 35 mm ISO 100-400. Why did you decide to use these particular films, and how did they affect the double exposures?

Laetitia: What I really like about these films is the fact that they give photos a surreal aesthetic that is fitting to my approach to double exposures. The unusual colors create a different perception of reality – almost as if learning to observe the world in a new way, to experience it for the first time.

Photos by Valentina Fernandez ( @valenfernandez)

A lot of participants also chose Lomography cameras for shooting. Which ones did they go for, and how did the type of camera influence the way they took pictures?

Laetitia: Some participants used the Sprocket Rocket. They would probably need to decide for themselves whether their choice of camera really impacted their photography. But in my workshop, the entire film was exposed twice, so that the process of double exposure already influenced the participants’ eye for photos. At the same time, I encouraged them to use the Splitzer and other creative filters – independent of the camera model.

Is there an image from the workshop that fascinates you particularly? If so, why that photo?

Laetitia: The results are quite impressive, especially for their first time. One image by Jose Licon Salaiz particularly stands out to me because it looks like the leaves' patterns are merging with the skin. That creates something hybrid between human and nature, which really appeals to me.

Photos by Stefan

To the participants: What did you think about the workshop? What are you taking away from it – for your photography and beyond?

Nina d'Hostel: The workshop was really interesting. I had wanted to learn the technique of double exposures for a while so that I could create poetic or unexpected compositions. I was happy to find out that you can leave compositions up to coincidence and spontaneity in double exposures, but you can also take notes about the first exposure to create an elaborate image or “painting”. Thanks to the Lomography films and this workshop, I was able to discover a new perspective in my photography, and now there are new methods and creative means to adopt and explore.

Ekaterina Shishko: The workshop was awesome! I especially liked the individual work with each participant and Laetitia's talent for languages – I’m impressed with her speaking three languages simultaneously. I didn’t dare to try double exposures in the past, but now I do. I feel more secure and relaxed because she explained everything so thoroughly. It was also cool to hold a Lomography camera in my hands for the first time. I really like the approach of Lomography and the rest of the analogue community, which embraces simplicity and accessibility for users. “Digital” communities simply cannot offer that – analogue is completely different. We also made friends with a lot of participants and already organized a photowalk – thank you for the networking, too!

It’s also important to mention that Laetitia didn’t seem arrogant at all when teaching us newbies about double exposure photography, despite her being such an expert! She was really patient and kind to everyone. Thank you for everything!

Photos by Jose Licon Salaiz ( antworteffekt)

What’s up for you next, both for the analogueNOW festival and for you personally, Laetitia?

Laetitia: At the moment, I mostly focus on the artistic work I'm doing as part of my residency. There, I continue to research the materiality of photography and am exploring it in an increasingly spatial sense. There are two solo exhibitions planned – one in June in Eckernförde and one next year in Flensburg – where I'll show the pieces I'm creating during this residency. I'm extending my photographs towards sculptural work and installations by combining RA-A-prints with other media, such as sewing, crocheting, stitching, and even video. Simultaneously, I am more and more interested in engaging with ecologically responsible photographic processes. I will also be a guest on the podcast “Fotopsychologisch” this summer.

Freia: After a short break in autumn, we’re going to start organizing next year’s analogueNOW festival. In the meantime, we’re collaborating with Photocentrum at Volkshochschule Berlin Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg. They are hosting several workshops about different analogue photography techniques, such as creating images without a camera through chemigrams, color-reversal processes, and X-ray film. We are currently organizing seven workshops in cooperation with Volkshochschule Berlin, taking place from mid-June until the end of September.

Photos 1–2: Nina d'Hostel ( @ninouhda) \| Photo 3: Ekaterina Shishko ( @bestiarubra)

We’d like to thank Laetitia, Freia, and all participants for the interview and this wonderful collaborative workshop, as well as the beautiful results! For more information about analogueNOW, visit their website or their Instagram page.

Hanyu Deng is a journalist, traveler, yoga enthusiast, and someone who still keeps a paper journal. She says it helps her slow down after days when her mind won’t stop running. We asked her to spend a day with the Lomo’Instant Automat and share what came of it. Here’s her take.

Photos by Hanyu Deng with the Lomo’Instant Automat

> Hi! I’m Hanyu Deng, freshly 32, and a journalist by trade. I love traveling, yoga, and journaling – they’re the things that help me truly switch off after long days when my brain’s been running nonstop. I’m drawn to the unknown, and I like to capture those moments in my journals. In a way, it’s not unlike my job: every day, I meet new people and get a glimpse into lives completely different from my own.

Photos from Hanyu Deng's vlog

> On the second day of May, I packed my journaling gear and the Lomo’Instant Automat, and met up with Liz at a café we’d been wanting to try for ages. Our plan? A whole afternoon of journaling – no phones, no distractions, just two people reclaiming a bit of real, tangible offline life.

> We always document our journaling sessions with photos, and later, those prints find their way into our spreads. It’s become our ritual. It’s funny how life works. She’s an ENFP, the golden-retriever type. I’m an INFJ. She’s Gen Z, a full six years younger than me. And yet, somehow, our tastes and sensibilities just click.

Photos from Hanyu Deng's vlog

> At the café, the first thing we did wasn’t order drinks – it was to spread our entire journaling kit across the table. Tape, stickers, scissors, tweezers, pens in every color, tickets, magazine cutouts. Liz showed me her latest finds: flyers from a journaling market, stand-up tickets, a stack of receipts, some printed photos, plus a few new treasures she’d just picked up.

> After a few sips of coffee, we moved on to the instant photos. The Lomo’Instant Automat handles metering automatically, all we had to do was press the shutter and wait. We shot quite a few that afternoon: one of me holding up my journal, writing the date, place, and event on the white border as it developed: “2026.5.02 Bella Café – journaling session with Liz.” Another of the two of us – I grabbed a marker and scribbled at the bottom: “The most important thing in life is to be happy,” added a few tiny stars and a sticker. Then one of me, smiling at the camera, holding the journal I’d filled up that day.

> We took our time decorating each print, matching stickers, jotting down where and when we were, who we were with, what we did. Sometimes we’d sketch our mood of the day. It felt like making something completely by hand, no presets, no templates, just however we felt at that moment. Compared to digital photos touched up with one tap, those crooked handwritten lines and tiny doodles on instant film actually feel more real.

Photos by Hanyu Deng with the Lomo’Instant Automat

> After we finished decorating the prints, we slipped into the quietest part of the afternoon: deep journaling mode. Liz started collaging photos from the week before, while I pasted the instant prints into that day’s spread. Soft background music played in the café. For a while, I stopped thinking about work, unfinished interviews, or the articles waiting to be written the next day. All my attention went into the texture of the collage, the flow of the words, where each photo should go. It felt almost like sinking into a deep, uninterrupted sleep – the outside world just fell away.

> Someone once asked me: “What goes through your mind when you’re journaling?” I thought about it, and said: “Nothing at all. It’s just relaxing.” I think journaling is one of the few things that lets me fully unwind completely, without reserve. It puts me in a flow state, as pleasant and restful as a deep sleep. These days, my phone barely holds my attention anymore. I've cut down on all that empty, glassy-eyed scrolling. Whenever I have a spare moment, I reach for my journal. My phone doesn’t stand a chance. And when I look at what I’ve finished, there’s a real sense of fulfillment, like I’ve actually made something. Journaling gives my overworked mind a proper rest. It fills me up. It’s a richer satisfaction than the hollow pleasure of endless short videos.

Photos by Hanyu Deng with the Lomo’Instant Automat (Product test – overexposed, but real enough.)

> That afternoon, neither of us touched our phones. No notifications, no short videos, no red dots from work chats. Just the rustle of scissors, the turning of pages, the occasional click and whir of instant film ejecting, and the easy back-and-forth chatter between us.

> When I got home and looked at the pages I’d finished that day – filled with photos, tape, and handwriting – I felt a quiet sense of satisfaction. I thought: journaling is my sanctuary. And the memories I’ve put down with my own hands will keep coming back to comfort me every time I open these pages in the future. Even if time forgets, my journal will remember.

Photo by Hanyu Deng with the Lomo’Instant Automat

Filmmaker James Trosh captured a historical moment on the streets of North London with the Sprocket Rocket when UK football team Arsenal, also known as The Gunners, celebrated their Premier League title and trophy on an open-top bus. The parade attracted a crowd of die-hard Arsenal fans dressed in their classic red shirts. You can almost hear the chants and cheers resonating from the photos. James talked to us about this special moment immortalized on this panoramic 35 mm point-and-shoot.

Photo by James Trosh with the Sprocket Rocket

Welcome to the Magazine, James! Could you give us a quick introduction about yourself and what you do?

I am a filmmaker and content producer from London, currently working in branded content. I've always loved experimenting with cameras – whether that's with an old dusty vintage camera or the latest innovations in camera technology. Back in 2010, I sent a GoPro on a weather balloon to the edge of space for a university project, kicking off the trend of floating random objects and an action camera up into the stratosphere.

More recently, I created one of the winning films in the Straight 8 film making challenge, an annual competition where filmmakers create a short film using a vintage Super 8 film camera on a single roll of Super 8 mm film, with no editing or chance to view the footage before the film is screened to the public. The first time I saw my film was at its premiere during the Straight 8 screening at the Cannes Film Festival.

Photo by James Trosh with the Sprocket Rocket

How did you get into film photography?

I've had an interest in film photography since growing up as a kid in the 90s – taking cheap disposable cameras with me on every family holiday, obsessing over the high-tech features of my parents' new APS camera as a teen, and investing in a Diana F+ camera to bring with me on a trip to Berlin as a university student.

It wasn't until I purchased a digital camera that emulated film stocks a couple of years ago that I fell back in love with the idea of film photography. I decided to purchase an old Soviet Zorki 1 rangefinder from a market in Budapest to start experimenting with real film again. Since then, my film camera collection has grown, and as someone who shares Lomography’s passion for experimenting with weird and wonderful cameras, it was only a matter of time before I added a few Lomography cameras to my arsenal. When I discovered the Sprocket Rocket, I knew it was a camera I wanted to find a use for straight away.

Photo by James Trosh with the Sprocket Rocket

Tell us about the day you spent with the camera. Where did you take it, and what did you decide to shoot?

I took the camera with me to the Arsenal Champions open-top bus parade in North London, to see the winning Arsenal team with the Premier League trophy. I wanted to capture the event in a different and unique way, as I knew the thousands of other fans there would all be capturing the same event with their mobile phone cameras. I found a great visually-interesting spot on the parade route opposite a group of fans who had taken over a block of houses with bold flags and bright red flares. After waiting a couple of hours, the bus approached, and I captured the team and the bus as they drove by.

Because the Sprocket Rocket takes extra-wide panoramic photos, I uploaded them to Instagram as a carousel, splitting the photos across multiple slides so viewers could swipe through the images as if manually moving down the film reel. My local film lab in Whitechapel developed the film and did a sprocket scan with a 24-hour turnaround, which meant I could upload the photos the day after the parade.

Photo by James Trosh with the Sprocket Rocket

How did you find the results from the Sprocket Rocket?

It was my first time using the camera. The delivery arrived a couple of days before the parade, and this was the first shoot I took it out on. It was very easy to use, I love the simplicity, and I was over the moon with the results. This event lent itself well to the wide-angled panoramic image frame – I was able to capture large groups of fans celebrating around the entire team bus.

Photo by James Trosh with the Sprocket Rocket

Any tips or thoughts you'd share with someone curious to try this camera for themselves?

The Sprocket Rocket's unique lens causes the far left and right edges of the frame to lose some focus and features some lens distortion. Try to find shots where you can keep your main subject in the center of the frame, while still framing your subject with an interesting surrounding to utilize the full width of the image. And make sure you find a film lab that can do a proper sprocket scan to utilize the full height of the image as well!

To see more of James' work, visit his Instagram page.

Few destinations captivate photographers quite like Japan. From the glowing lights of its cities to the tranquility of its forests and mountains, the country’s charm has long left a lasting impression on all who visit. Lomographer Stephen Hutchison ( @stephenhutchison) experienced this firsthand during a two-week family vacation across Tokyo, Kamakura, Hakone, Kyoto, and Fujikawaguchiko.

In this edition of Around the World in Analogue, we're heading to the Land of the Rising Sun as we welcome Stephen back to the Magazine to share two weeks of family adventures and solitary wanderings in Japan.

Credits: @stephenhutchison \| M: LomoChrome Turquoise 35 mm ISO 100–400

Name: Stephen Hutchison

LomoHome: @stephenhutchison

Social media: stephenhutchison

Camera: Leica M6 TTL, Pentax 17

Film: Ilford HP5 400, Ilford Delta 3200, LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400, LomoChrome Turquoise 35 mm ISO 100–400

Location: Tokyo, Kamakura, Hakone, Kyoto, Fujikawaguchiko

Last April, our family took a trip to Japan. My wife and I planned this trip to celebrate our birthdays, which fall a week apart. We also wanted to take one last flight with our daughter before she turned two and would soon need her own ticket.

We decided to travel light, so I packed just two film cameras: Leica M6 and Pentax 17. In addition, I packed forty rolls of film. I usually bring more cameras and film rolls, but I have become frustrated with the repetitive nature of my photographs over the years. I often end up capturing the same image multiple times with different cameras and film stocks.

While preparing for this trip, I was reminded of my first photography trip to Mexico when I brought only one camera and one type of film. When I returned home, I was struck by how focused and cohesive this body of work was. So on this Japan trip, I resisted the urge to bring anything else that would add complexity – I would only carry a baby stroller, diaper backpack, and two cameras.

Credits: @stephenhutchison \| UR: LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400, LL: LomoChrome Turquoise 35 mm ISO 100–400

In two x-ray-safe bags, I packed four different film stocks: Ilford HP5+ 400, Ilford Delta 3200, LomoChrome Purple 400, and LomoChrome Turquoise 400 – I decided on these only after confirming our itinerary. We bought our rail passes before traveling and mapped a two-week route, starting and ending in Tokyo.

Our daughter loves trains, and we often ride a small historic children’s train at Griffith Park back home. Throughout our trip, my wife and I shared our daughter’s innate ability to notice the beauty and serenity outside our windows while we travelled by bullet trains, ropeways, and cable cars.

Credits: stephenhutchison

After walking all day, my wife and daughter would fall asleep in the evening. Meanwhile, I would take my film and cameras, then head out in search of bright lights, long shadows, and the sensation of being slightly lost. I loaded Ilford Delta 3200 film and photographed the city until the early morning as it looked both asleep and awake.

I learned the hard way that the train system shuts down in many places when it’s very late at night. I realized this while shooting a mirrored escalator tunnel in Shinjuku. It was just after three in the morning, and I was more than ten miles from where I would eventually need to sleep for a few hours.

From Tokyo, we took the train to Kamakura, a quaint but cool beach town that almost reminded us of Venice Beach back home. I loaded LomoChrome Turquoise 400 film and photographed at the beach. Along the shore, I planned for the blue sky to shift to a deep orange, and the sand to take on a pale bluish hue. I looked for figures walking along the water’s edge, families and groups of children, slightly indistinguishable and distant on the sand.

Credits: @stephenhutchison \| D: LomoChrome Turquoise 35 mm ISO 100–400

After spending some time near the beach, we traveled by train to Hakone. I photographed the mountains, each speckled with dots marking sporadic cherry blossom trees. It felt slightly roguish to photograph the nearly sacred cherry blossom trees with color-shifting film, but I was excited by this quietly rebellious act.

Throughout our time there, we hiked heavily wooded trails, sometimes flanked by columns of volcanic steam. In the mornings, while my wife and daughter slept, I photographed on the trails. I followed warm rivers that fed creeks and navigated tunnels under bridges and past abandoned homes. I was mesmerized by the makeshift network of pipes that brought warm water directly to each house.

Credits: @stephenhutchison \| LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400

One of my most memorable photographing experiences was when we took a ropeway up Owakudai, “The Great Boiling Valley”. I felt like James Nachtwey in the documentary “War Photographer.” I photographed the harsh, rigid, and carved landscape with columns of steam escaping from the earth.

I first loaded my cameras with black-and-white film and tried to familiarize myself fully with the environment. Once I was confident that I had explored this space without color, I loaded Lomochrome Turquoise and caught the more ominous-looking scenes to contrast with the bright and playful colorfulness of the film.

We ended our stay in Hakone with a trip to the POLA Museum of Art, which quickly became one of my favorite museums. Behind the museum, we walked a long, winding trail in search of the Roni Horn sculpture I wanted to photograph. I shot rolls of LomoChrome Purple and Turquoise, alternating between photographing my family and the sculptural works that meandered through the forest behind the museum.

Credits: @stephenhutchison \| M: LomoChrome Turquoise 35 mm ISO 100–400

On one final early morning in Hakone, we woke up and took several trains to Kyoto. It was here, while walking the streets at night, that I truly fell in love with Japan. I searched for dimly lit alleys, as I did in Tokyo, but was most drawn to explore the banks of the Kamo River. I photographed groups of people as they settled along the river. Friends, colleagues, and lovers each lay out their blankets – some played music, others played card games.

I enjoyed photographing at night, and without a tripod, I rested my cameras on electrical boxes and benches while trying to capture the occasional motion blur. My favorite time to photograph is just before dusk. I was fortunate that this was also when the river and its banks were most active.

Credits: stephenhutchison

After spending several days in Kyoto, we traveled to Fujikawaguchiko – a small mountainside town perched next to a lake with mostly unobstructed views of Mt. Fuji. We enjoyed this small town and walked for hours along the lake, photographing cherry blossoms along the shore and the pirate ship that occasionally crossed behind the mountains.

In the mornings, I hiked trails and photographed the misty pathways with LomoChrome Purple, then brought breakfast back for my family. On one rainy day, we decided to visit a quirky amusement park nestled in the hills. The park, called Fuji-Q Highland, was nearly empty. I photographed the roller coasters looking dormant in the rain under grey, gloomy skies.

Credits: @stephenhutchison \| M: LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400

Finally, we traveled back to Tokyo to spend a few final days shopping, eating, and photographing. While reflecting on our family trip and the collection of photos I have taken, I can confirm that there is a slight sadness that exists within someone who has visited and returned home from Japan. I feel fortunate that I was able to postpone this feeling for at least three or four days while I processed and scanned nearly forty rolls of film.

I feel grateful that I was prepared to photograph Japan exactly as I experienced it. I packed the right film for late-night, low-light excursions, for dramatic urban scenes, and for natural forested trails.

Credits: @stephenhutchison \| UR, LL: LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400

For anyone planning to photograph in Japan:

First, it was easy to find film, but the era of low-cost, mint cameras seems to be over. I have heard of stores stacked floor to ceiling with low-cost cameras, but I went to more than a dozen camera stores and was never satisfied with either price or selection.

Second, I would suggest buying a rail pass that covers the duration of your trip. We found amazing photo trips easily without having to worry about buying separate train tickets each time.

Lastly, I would encourage everyone to observe and take note of any customs or traditions before photographing. At times, there are places, activities, and people that are not necessarily meant to be photographed. I found this most true at certain shrines, observing ceremonies, or visiting cemeteries. Most specifically, I did not photograph people while they engaged in religious observation or moments that seemed too sacred.

We'd like to thank Stephen for sharing his images and his travel journey with us! Make sure to follow his LomoHome and Instagram if you'd like to see more of his work.

Want to take us Around the World in Analogue? Send your entry to [magazine-submission@lomography.com](mailto:magazine-submission@lomography.com) with the subject line: Around the World in Analogue and tell us all about your travel destinations. Read the guidelines here.
