What's it like to be a film shutterbug living in some of the most well-known, iconic cities in the world? Our new series explores these cities through the eyes of local Lomographers, who share emerging, classic, and underrated art, music, food and historical spots, for anyone looking to immerse themselves in the soul of the sprawling metropolis.

We now have over 100 (and counting...) Travel Guides on our website, full of photography and travel inspiration tips around the globe. This time, we thought that we would let Lomographers themselves give us all the pieces we needed to create a Travel Guide for the tangolicious city of Buenos Aires.

Credits: mariamariasol & juliangarcia

We find ourselves in the Southern Hemisphere, in a city that is the Bookstore capital of the world, has a 67-meter tall condom and is where Pope Francis used to be a bouncer. Its European influences show themselves in Buenos Aires’ plazas, elegant buildings and a lovely balance of arts, delicious cafes, and nightlife. The Tango, a dance meant to knock both your socks and pants off, originated in the working class neighborhoods of the city.

Let’s dive into this vibrant city with the help of Lomographers María Sol ( @mariamariasol) and Julián Garcia ( @juliangarcia). We reached out to them after finding their LomoHome in our global Community. We sent over a list of questions and asked for their recommendations for the city they call home.

Credits: mariamariasol & juliangarcia

Hi María and Julián, welcome to Lomography Magazine. Where do you currently reside, and how did you start taking film photography?

María: I currently live in Buenos Aires City, the capital of Argentina, in the area of Parque Patricios. I started taking analogue photos thanks to a friend of my sister who was actively involved in analogue photography and inspired me. She then sold me her first camera, a Canon EOS 1000FN, and I loved it. I had been taking photos with a digital camera since I was twelve, but the art of analogue photography truly changed my life. My father and grandmother always had an analogue camera in hand, and there are many family memories associated with it, which also greatly inspired me to dedicate myself to analogue photography.

Julián: I currently reside in Vicente López, which is a suburb in the north of Buenos Aires. It is also the neighborhood I lived in for most of my life, and where I started taking film photography. In 2019, I decided to buy my first camera, a 1962 Voigtländer Bessamatic, bought in a small store on Libertad street. Through some YouTube videos, the original instruction manual and tips from my father, I learnt how to operate the camera and shot my first roll. It was a Kodak Pro Image shot around the house and the neighborhood.

Credits: juliangarcia

What is it like becoming a film photographer in your city? Would you say there’s a strong film culture?

María: Actually, I would describe it as an ambiguous feeling. On one hand, I feel like I want and need to capture as much as I can; it's a beautiful city full of capturable moments and places.

And on the other hand, because I'm a perfectionist, I also don't want to recreate what already exists, and I try to avoid being influenced by what I've already seen. But I also believe that no two eyes are alike, and we need all kinds of eyes imaginable in order to have multiple perspectives on the world. Otherwise, everything would be the same...

Credits: mariamariasol

So, if I had to answer this question again, I would say that I feel very fortunate to live here and to capture this timeline with my own eyes. I love my country and I'm very proud of it, even when circumstances are complex. I would say that Argentina has a very strong film culture and many great creative minds. The artistic quality here is truly amazing, not only in photography, but also in film, theater, painting, music, and much more. We have a huge variety of options for all tastes. Argentina is a country with a great cultural influence, and the University of Buenos Aires is one of the best universities in Latin America, so we have excellent professionals.

Credits: mariamariasol

Julián: Thankfully, it is not a struggle. In Buenos Aires, you have access to many traditional photography stores, modern labs, and countless second-hand cameras. I am sure there are other big cities in Argentina that do not have easy access to these services, so film photography becomes cumbersome if you do not develop yourself.

What’s your gear like? Are there any cameras or film stocks that stand out to you, especially in relation to photographing your city?

María: I own four analogue cameras – Canon EOS 1000FN, Voigtländer VF135, Olympus Trip MD2, and Zenit-E – and I like to use each one to achieve different looks. My latest discovery was extra-sensitive film because Buenos Aires is a nocturnal city, and I love how the lights look with a Cinestill 800T or Portra 800, for example. I'm currently testing an Ilford Delta 3200, because I love how black and white film makes everything look, especially in low light.

Julián: With the Bessamatic, I got really used to shooting its 50 mm f2.8 ColorSkopar and 135 mm f4, but other lenses were rare or too expensive. That is why I decided to get a Nikon F2 with a 50 mm f/1.4 AIS. This lens is really useful for the low light indoor conditions I currently have to photograph.

I believe there is an interesting side of Buenos Aires that happens late at night, which makes it hard to photograph. This is why I like using any 400 ISO black and white film stock, preferably HP5 or Tri-X, and push it to 1600 or even 3200 ISO.

Credits: mariamariasol & juliangarcia

Where do you usually hang out? Could you share favorite spots which might be considered underrated?

María: I often hang out with my friends in the historic San Telmo district. It's a pleasant place because you can be out on the street and there are many popular bars. Furthermore, it is a beautiful neighborhood, thanks to its infrastructure, which preserves its emblematic cobblestone streets. The atmosphere there is different from that of more upscale areas of the city, like the area of Palermo.

Lezama Park is one of my favorite places, not only for its enormous green space, but also for the flea market that opens every Saturday, full of incredible treasures. And I'd say that, although it's a bit underrated, it's one of the best parks in the city.

Credits: mariamariasol – San Telmo district, Buenos Aires

Another place my friends and I like to go at night is YÖBLA bar in San Telmo, which delights us with its excellent music selection and reasonably priced drinks.

The Microcentro area, more specifically Plaza General San Martín, is also one of my favorite places for taking photos, strolling, and much more. It's surrounded by beautiful buildings and charming cafes. At sunset, you can enjoy Dada bar, located just around the corner from one of the city's most emblematic buildings: the Kavanagh Building.

Credits: mariamariasol & juliangarcia

Julián: I guess my usual spot right now would be Saldias Centro Cultural. This place, which used to be an abandoned fruit market, turned into a huge complex of rehearsal rooms. Here, local bands can rent the room monthly and rehearse whenever they want. On the weekends, some bands might play live on the stage inside the complex. So, you can go listen to the band playing or knock on a random rehearsal room to listen to another band playing and they (most likely) won’t mind.

Credits: juliangarcia – Saldias Polo Cultural, Buenos Aires

What is your favorite photo walk route in your city?

María: I usually like to simply let myself be carried away by the impulse to go somewhere I've never been and take my camera with me, although sometimes it's hard for me to leave my comfort zone, I try to do it as much as possible by choosing different streets that I've never walked before. I simply get inspired by observing and imagining how the photo would look after taking it and I simply take long walks. But if I had to choose, I would always go for Microcentro, Plaza de Mayo, Florida, Retiro, districts that are very close to each other, because I simply love the architecture and the light is very harmonious.

Starting at Plaza de Mayo and heading straight to Reconquista Street, where you'll find Clorindo Testa's brutalist-style Banco Hipotecario – formerly the Bank of London – I like to simply wander and discover things I may never have noticed before.

Credits: juliangarcia & mariamariasol

Julián: When I walk around the city to take photos I prefer to be spontaneous and to have a slower pace. This is why I usually just go out with a camera during the day and walk around places like Vicente López, Belgrano or Saavedra without having a specific route or destination.

I like those neighborhoods because they feel quieter and less hectic than the city center. I rarely go out looking for a specific image. Usually, I just walk until something catches my attention. For this purpose, I believe any 100 or 200 ISO color or black and white film will work beautifully.

Have you taken any photos of your city that you consider your favorite? What’s the story behind it?

Credits: mariamariasol – Catalinas Sur in La Boca district, Buenos Aires

María: I think this is one of my favorite photos taken in Buenos Aires. The thing about this photo is that I had just bought a second-hand Voigtländer VF135 and was testing it out when my sister told me she had the perfect spot for me to take the remaining shots on my roll of film. So she took me to the Catalinas Sur towers, which is a unique residential enclave within La Boca, and looks beautiful from any angle. It has twenty towers, or “monoblocks,” and a number of chalets from the 1960s. The man in the photo was contemplating the beautiful summer afternoon with his dog, and I found him fascinating.

Credits: juliangarcia – Diagonal Norte, Buenos Aires

Julián: Even though it is slightly faulty from one of my first attempts at developing film, I would say this is my favorite photo of my city. I especially like it because it captures the context of the city center, which always changes rapidly. It is the only picture I took where you can instantly tell it was taken in Buenos Aires. This was shot on Diagonal Norte, facing the Obelisco on 9 de Julio, with the band Daltónica in the frame.

A Call to Our Community

We are constantly expanding our Travel Guides and would love your help. Just like with María and Julián in Buenos Aires, we want to hear your perspective, tips and tricks for the city you call home. If you feel like a city is missing, reach out to us at travel@lomography.com. We can't wait to hear from you!

In music, image is almost as important as sound. It helps build an artist’s universe, extends the emotional resonance of their work, and shapes how they are perceived. Yet in an era defined by instant content and ultra-polished visuals, a growing number of photographers are returning to film as a way of documenting musicians differently, embracing texture, presence, and a degree of unpredictability.

That is precisely what the photography collective Argenteurs explores through their projects. On one hand, capturing the raw energy of the live show of Sébastien Tellier with the Lomo MC-A; on the other, creating a shot meant to last: the cover of the single Camavinga by CMARG, shot on Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400. Two very different approaches to music photography, united by a shared ambition: to create images that feel alive, sensitive, and deeply embodied.

Credits: Argenteurs \| Left: Shot with the Lomo MC-A, Right: Shot with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

Hello, Argenteurs! We’re delighted to welcome you back for another interview. How have you been since our last conversation ?

Very well, thank you. How about you?

Quite a lot has happened since our last interview. One of the highlights was presenting our South In Paris exhibition at Fisheye Gallery, a project we had been developing for several years and one that marked an important milestone for us. Alongside that, we’ve continued to grow our commercial work across music, sports, and fashion, while still making time for our personal projects.

We remain committed to bringing our images beyond the screen through exhibitions and print collections. At the moment, we’re presenting Dérives – Alteration as a Reinterpretation of Reality at Fracas Paris. The series stems from our fascination with the unexpected in analogue photography. Through this project, we explore how chance can transform the way we see and reveal alternative readings of reality. It’s an invitation to embrace what escapes our control and to welcome the detours and imperfections that shape our images just as much as they shape our lives. If you have the opportunity, we’d love for you to discover the exhibition, either at Fracas Paris until June 23rd or on our website.

Credits: Argenteurs \| Shot with the Lomo MC-A

With the concert of Sébastien Tellier and the cover you created for CMARG, you've recently worked on two projects closely connected to music. What draws you to the way film photography captures artists and their worlds?

We love music for how deeply human and embodied it is. Even when artists enjoy crafting a certain image of themselves, music remains something incredibly personal and emotionally charged. That's what inspires us and what makes us press the shutter when that sense of authenticity resonates with us. Artists are also constantly evolving, and there's an archival dimension to our work that means a lot to us. Whenever we photograph an artist, whether in the studio, on stage, or during more intimate moments, we're always thinking about preserving a tangible trace of that particular moment in time. A roll of film almost becomes a form of memory, capturing an artist at a specific point in their journey.

Beyond music itself, shooting on film is simply how we work. It's a choice that's deeply rooted in our vision of photography, the creative process, and the physical nature of the image. Even though photographing concerts on film is definitely not the easiest route, haha. We often joke about it with digital photographers, who can constantly adjust their settings, shoot hundreds of frames, review their images instantly, and move on. Meanwhile, we're working with 36 exposures and a roll of film that never seems to have enough light. But those limitations push us to experiment differently, and often lead to images with a very distinct character and personality.

Do you feel that artists today are more receptive to film photography and what it conveys?

Yes, that's definitely something we've noticed. A lot of artists today are looking for something more organic and tangible in the way they're represented.

We live in an environment saturated with screens, content, and images produced at an incredible pace. That constant flood naturally leads some artists to reconnect with practices that feel more grounded in reality and in the physicality of their work. Film also brings a certain imperfection that stands in contrast to the highly polished, tightly controlled aesthetic we often see today. Many artists appreciate that quality precisely because it feels alive, less predictable, and more human. That doesn't mean digital photography is any less interesting. On the contrary, it opens up countless creative possibilities. Photography today is wonderfully diverse, with very different approaches that can coexist perfectly, and we think that's a very positive thing.

Credits: Argenteurs \| Shot with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

But we have definitely noticed that more and more musicians are drawn to the organic quality of film photography, and that sensibility is reflected in many of today's artistic directions. The rise of generative AI is also part of this broader conversation. For some artists, choosing to work with tangible photography, created through a recognizable craft and process, is a way of staying consistent with their views on issues that are now shaping artistic disciplines across the board.

These two projects took very different approaches: on one hand, a live concert; on the other, a more carefully crafted single cover. Can you tell us about the creative process behind each project? How did your approach differ?

We like to describe it as the difference between fishing for images and cultivating them. With a concert, everything is far more spontaneous. You're discovering a venue, a stage design, lighting, and a performance that are constantly evolving. At Sébastien Tellier's concert, we had to work with the moving set pieces, his movements across the stage, his interactions with the audience, the changing light, and all the little moments that make a live show feel alive. A lot of the time is spent with your eye pressed to the viewfinder, observing what's happening and releasing the shutter when you feel a moment deserves to be preserved.

Credits: Argenteurs \| Shot with the Lomo MC-A

For a cover image, the process is almost the opposite. As with the project for CMARG, we start by imagining an image that extends the world of the music and the artist. That means there's a lot of thinking, discussion, and collaboration with the artist's team before we even pick up a camera. In this particular case, the song referenced Camavinga, who also happens to be CMARG's son's idol. She wanted to incorporate that personal connection into the image. We came up with a scene in which her son is seen from behind, wearing a French player's jersey that's slightly too big for him: a way of evoking those childhood dreams that always seem bigger than ourselves. We also wanted the image to feel bright and summery, in keeping with the energy of the track. Once the concept was established, all that remained was to bring it to life, experiment with different shots during the shoot, and then present several options to the artist once the film had been developed and scanned.

Credits: Argenteurs \| Shot with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

For the series shot during Sébastien Tellier's concert, what made you want to use the Lomo MC-A? Was there something about its rendering or the way it shoots that felt particularly suited to the energy of the moment?

We're always curious to try out new cameras, and the release of the Lomo MC-A seemed like the perfect opportunity to put it through its paces in real-world conditions. What immediately appealed to us was its compact size and responsiveness. The autofocus is especially useful in a concert setting, where everything changes very quickly. Its 32 mm f/2.8 lens also makes it possible to work without a flash in conditions that can sometimes be quite challenging. As we mentioned earlier, artists move around a lot during a live show, and the ability to adjust the shutter speed is another major advantage compared to many point-and-shoot compacts. It gives you much more control when it comes to freezing the action. The exposure compensation feature is also a welcome addition in a concert environment, where lighting conditions can vary dramatically from one song to the next.

To be honest, we loaded a roll into it without any particular expectations for this first outing, and it ended up producing several of our favorite images from the evening. For the record, all of the black-and-white photographs in this series were shot with the MC-A.

Credits: Argenteurs \| Shot with the Lomo MC-A

A live concert inevitably involves a great deal of spontaneity, which only adds to the unpredictability of shooting on film. How did that influence the way you approached photographing it?

Photographing a concert on film means dealing with a huge number of variables: the venue, access restrictions, lighting, the artists' movements, and often very limited light. They're not the most comfortable conditions for shooting film, but that's exactly what makes it so rewarding. We only press the shutter when we genuinely feel that something meaningful is happening. It requires a lot of attention, anticipation, and observation.

The unpredictability is also part of the fun. Every time we take a picture, we have an idea of what the image might look like, but it's almost never exactly what we'll discover once the film is developed. That can be frustrating at times, but more than anything, it leaves room for surprise and that's something we really enjoy. Concerts also tend to last long enough to allow for experimentation. The goal isn't to make the same image 36 times, but to try different settings, different framings, and different ways of working with the light.

We often laugh about it because after every concert, people ask us whether we managed to get the shots we were hoping for. And our answer is always the same: we'll find out during development, haha! Even after several years, there's still an element of the unknown. But in the end, we almost always come away with images that we love and that the artists love, too. So, we keep going.

By contrast, the cover image for the single Camavinga feels much more carefully constructed. How did you develop that image with the artist?

The image grew out of our conversations with CMARG about the song and the story she wanted to tell visually. The reference to Camavinga was central to the track, but there was also a much more personal layer to it, since he's her son's favourite player. We built the image around that idea by placing her son at the centre of the composition. We wanted something simple, sincere, and symbolic, an image that could extend the meaning of the song without slipping into a literal interpretation of it.

Credits: Argenteurs \| Shot with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

Why did you choose the Lomography Color Negative 400 film for this project?

We were looking for a versatile colour film that could reproduce natural tones while still offering a rich and vibrant colour palette. Since the track has a very summery energy, we wanted the image to feel bright, warm, and colourful without becoming overly artificial. Lomography Color Negative ISO 400 was a perfect fit for what we had in mind. It's a relatively neutral film stock that leaves plenty of room for interpretation in the final image while still delivering beautiful color vibrancy. Its fairly fine grain was also a major advantage, since we knew the image would be cropped and used as cover artwork. Once again, it performed exactly the way we needed it to for this project!

Which photograph, or photographs, from these series is your favorite?

For the CMARG cover, our favorite image is also the one that was ultimately chosen by the artist. It's always nice when everyone ends up on the same page!

Credits: Argenteurs \| Shot with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

When it comes to Sébastien Tellier, one of our favourites is the colour shot of his entrance onto the stage. His silhouette emerges through the smoke, almost as if stepping out of a dream, surrounded by the musicians performing alongside him.

We're also particularly fond of a portrait taken with the Lomo MC-A in which he's adjusting his cap. There's a slight motion blur that captures the energy of the live performance, while the moment itself remains beautifully frozen in time. His face is hidden in shadow, but his shoes, jacket, and cap sparkle like stars, leaving no doubt as to who the true focal point of the image is.

Credits: Argenteurs \| Shot with the Lomo MC-A

Finally, are there any upcoming projects you would like to share with our readers?

We have quite a few projects in progress, both commercial and personal, so the easiest way to follow them is probably through our Instagram or our website, where everything is constantly evolving.

The Dérives series we mentioned earlier is already available on our website, with several prints currently for sale. To conclude, we are currently working on a rather ambitious editorial project in collaboration with another artist. Without revealing too much for now, it brings together different aesthetics, different eras, and different mediums, shot using a 9x12 large format camera from the 1930s. It will be presented in the autumn as an exhibition, and continues the reflection that has long guided our work: reaffirming the central role of the materiality of the image and fully analogue craftsmanship.

A big thank you to Argenteurs for taking the time to answer our questions. To discover more of their world and check out their upcoming events, feel free to follow them on Instagram or visit their website.

What does instant photography bring to a lifelong journaling practice? For Brooklyn-based artist Cat Caldarola, ( @talllcatart) creativity has always been intertwined with collecting memories. Raised among family photo albums, scrapbooks, and sketchbooks, they now combine printmaking, textiles, photography, and journaling into a deeply personal creative practice.

We spoke with Cat about documenting everyday moments, the joy of working with instant film, and why physical journals remain some of the most meaningful records of a life. With the Lomo'Instant Wide Glass in hand, they captured moments from their creative practice. Browse through a selection of pages from their Analogue Journal and read our conversation below.

Art created by Cat Caldarola ( @talllcatart)

Hey, Cat, welcome to Lomography Magazine! Can you tell us a little about yourself?

My name is Cat, and I am a 24-year-old artist located in Brooklyn, NY. I have been printmaking since 2019, but I've made art for as long as I can remember. I grew up around a dad who took a ton of photos and a mom who would scrapbook those photographs into decorative albums recounting our lives. When I was old enough, my dad taught me how to use his camera, and my mom took me along on her scrapbooking weekends (imagine a school auditorium full of 45+-year-old women, and me). I was one of those little kids who had a journal collection. Every single one was opened, all barely used, but each one served a purpose only I knew about.

I cannot pretend that my journal collection now does not mimic that of 10-year-old Cat. At least now, I think they're all being put to good use. I’ve been pursuing art in any form that inspired me, so my work spans across mediums. Currently, I have reconnected with my love of textile art, which was ignited by my aunt, who taught me to quilt in my early teens. These inspirations have led me to an interesting crossover between lino printing and lace making!

Art and Photos created by Cat Caldarola ( @talllcatart)

What usually ends up in your journal?

It completely depends on what kind of journal I am keeping at that moment. I've had journals devoted solely to keeping trash (affectionately named junk), or ones designated to keep up with K-pop idols back when I was 14. I’ve been keeping some kind of bullet journal or planner for over 10 years now, and I find it integral to keeping me organized, productive, and creative.

Sketchbooks that span years and journals full of emotions, poems, and photos litter the space under my bed. At 24, my two main journals keep track of my emotions and my art. But to answer your question, anything and everything ends up in my journals. If it can fit, I’ll stick whatever it is in with some double-sided tape and call it a day.

Art and Photos created by Cat Caldarola ( @talllcatart)

Does your journal hold a different kind of memory than what you share online?

Most of my journals feel distinctly personal, even when I share them online. The memory I have of a moment will sometimes differ from the emotions I portray in a journal spread. I like that part of sharing my journal with other people. No matter the medium of the contents, I like to see how others interpret what I have made. Sketchbooks are particularly fun in that sense.

Art is almost always interpreted differently than how you might've meant it. But every single journal or sketchbook I’ve had, no matter how much I may have shared it online, has a feeling to me that no one else can grasp. I think that’s the most special part of keeping these physical documents of your life. They are free shots of nostalgia whenever you want them.

Art and Photos created by Cat Caldarola ( @talllcatart)

How does instant photography change the way you document memories?

Instant photography was sort of a life-changer when it comes to documenting my memories. I have always had trouble keeping up with the number of memories I wish to highlight in my journals and scrapbooks. When the photo is in my hands instantly, I get to keep up with the creative process I had in my head instead of stalling until I can print the photos I want.

I enjoyed romanticizing my process through the lens. Typically, my days can be pretty similar: carving, editing, printing, sleeping, eating, rinse, repeat. But with a camera, I was able to take a second to explore the beauty in those moments I take for granted a lot of the time. Doing what I love for as long as I want. I really enjoyed implementing instant photography into my practice, and I hope to do so more in the future!

Do you have a favorite spread or page from this journal? What's the story behind it?

I think my favorite spread would have to be the cyanotype pages. I had such fun that day, boiling on my roof, running up and down the steps to get fresh water to rinse my prints. I enjoyed the experimentation behind it, reminding me very much of being in a darkroom and developing film. The cyanotype sheets had been a Christmas gift from my brother, and I have enjoyed putting them to good use. It’s always exciting to me when a new hobby becomes a thing I want to invest time and energy into. The delicious lace texture and crisp blue hues were so satisfying to me that I didn't even mind getting a little sunburned.

Art and Photos created by Cat Caldarola ( @talllcatart)

--

Thanks, Cat, for chatting with us and creating such a beautiful journal. Make sure to check out their work on Instagram!

Subway stations are perhaps not the most popular photo spots, but Czech photographer David, also known as Dami1992), definitely makes the most of them. Aside from the inspiration he draws from shooting in liminal spaces, he talks to us about his technical preferences for photography. This photo selection documents his first encounter with Lomography films, and later, he shares a glimpse of what might come next.

© @Dami1992 \| Film: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Hello, David! Welcome to Lomography. Could you please introduce yourself?

Hi, I’m Dami1992, a photographer from Prague, and I love shooting urban landscapes, street photography, and travel photography. My guilty pleasure is photographing metro systems around the world, brutalist architecture, and liminal space photography.

© @Dami1992 \| Film: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

When did you start shooting on film? Do you remember what the beginning of your passion for analogue looked like?

I recently sought an answer to this question myself, and I took my first film photos as a child in 2002. Back then, my parents gave me their old point-and-shoot camera with one roll of film for a school trip. I even preserved the photos; in most of the 36 shots, my fingers are in the lens! But if we move from my early childhood analogue photography to my current work, I gradually began to lean more towards analogue photography from 2024, when I started feeling that I wanted to take my photography to the next level. Since 2025, I have been shooting only on analogue.

© @Dami1992 \| Film: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

You tend to photograph dark, liminal spaces – what draws you to these areas?

Yes, it’s definitely my guilty pleasure...I don’t know why, but these spaces have always attracted me; they have a strange charm. I enjoy the architecture of the individual metro stations, but also how the metro spaces change from a noisy transit area bustling with thousands of people during the day to a place where, as the day progresses, it becomes quieter with only the sounds of escalators, fluorescent lights, or water dripping from the walls.

I love noticing individual details and differences; have you ever noticed that each metro system has its specific smell? The underground has a completely different charm for me than life above ground, which is why I enjoy seeking it out in my work. Another reason I often look for subways to shoot is that you can photograph there almost non-stop; a photographer isn’t dependent on weather or lighting conditions. The metro simply has its soul and an unmistakable charm.

© @Dami1992 \| Film: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

High ISO is a must when capturing such scenes. How did you find working with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800 ?

I worked great with this film. Since I hate tripods and always shoot all my photos handheld, ISO 800 is a must for me in these spaces. I liked the results I achieved with this film; I was surprised by the pleasant grain and the way colors were rendered. In my opinion, this is the ideal film for nighttime street photography, subway shooting, or shooting in poor lighting conditions.

© @Dami1992 \| Film: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

If you could give this film stock a soundtrack, which song would capture its mood and texture?

That would definitely be a track by Sub Focus - “Enter Night”! As the title suggests, this film opens new possibilities, especially in the evening and in poor lighting conditions, so this song fits perfectly with it, just like with my shooting style.

What is it that makes you choose film instead of digital solutions?

The digital form of photography started to bore me. I have a digital setup worth thousands of euros, where the focus never misses, and the camera has dozens of megapixels, but over time, it started to lack soul. It became too easy for me to take photos; making a bad photo with this setup is practically impossible. I started looking for a direction to push my work, and thanks to film, I feel that my photos have more emotions and that I enjoy the overall process of shooting analogue much more.

© @Dami1992 \| Film: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

I enjoy learning new techniques, being able to read light, and estimating the distance to the subject instead of just pressing the autofocus button on the camera body. I’d say I’m returning from high-end technical photography back to the roots of photography, and that’s something that excites and fulfills me. I also started traveling a lot more, and due to compactness and weight, film is a much more pleasant choice for me.

You enjoy street photography, too. Do you have any tips on how to photograph strangers?

Haha, that’s quite a controversial topic, right? I’d probably recommend everyone to respect the environment and the person they’re photographing. Personally, I never try to photograph people in uncomfortable moments or situations where I wouldn’t want to be photographed myself. It’s also good to listen to your inner intuition; if I sense that I’m in an environment where it doesn’t feel appropriate, I won’t go for it. At first, I’d recommend photographing silhouettes or people from behind, or focusing on details of their outfits.

© @Dami1992 \| Film: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

Many photos that capture a specific detail of a person, like a close-up of a hand with a cigarette and an interesting tattoo, or details of an outfit, interest me more than a meaningless close-up of someone’s face. A photographer should also be prepared for confrontation while shooting; 95% of ordinary people outside of photographers don’t actually know what street photography is, and it’s our job to ensure that the photographed person never leaves with a negative experience of us as photographers.

Explain to them why you took their photo, perhaps because you were attracted to their nice outfit, compliment them on it, and try to make their day better. You should always have respect for the other side and show your positive side as a photographer.

© @Dami1992 \| Film: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

How would you describe your process as a photographer? Is it spontaneous or rather more intentional?

Interesting question! When I think about it, it’s influenced by the locations where I shoot. In my city, which I know like the back of my hand, I’m 99% spontaneous. However, when I travel, I plan my itinerary quite a bit, deciding on the locations I want to visit, and I generally have a fixed plan that I follow, using the time between transfers to other locations for spontaneous shooting. Of course, if I discover something that catches my eye along the way, I have no problem with spontaneous shooting, but I’m usually more of a planning-type photographer.

There is always room to try out new things. Are there any products from Lomography that you would like to try out in the future?

Definitely! I’m currently getting into black-and-white photography and plan to try out more black-and-white films from Lomography. I really enjoyed the output from the 800 ISO film and also from the Lomography Color Negative ISO 400, which accompanied me on the street for the last few days, and to which I will definitely return. I’m currently intrigued by the LomoChrome Color '92 Sun-kissed ISO 400 because summer is starting, and this type of film looks ideal for summer shooting!

© @Dami1992 \| Film: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

If you had to pick one favorite shot you’ve taken with Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400, which one would it be and what makes it special to you?

I don’t like this! With every captured photo, I usually have some memory, and it’s hard for me to choose just one. But in this case, it would probably be a photo of a woman carrying her child while her shadow is reflected. I have a deep connection to this place; I really love the architecture and the lines of the surroundings because it was built by my favorite architect, Karel Prager.

Additionally, it’s a creative environment for me; there’s a café in that building where I’ve spent hours editing photos and writing blogs about photography, observing urban life, light play, and enjoying my existence in an urban environment.

© @Dami1992 \| Film: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

It is safe to say that you love photographing subway stations. I need to know – what was your favorite subway to capture on film?

Each subway system is unique to me; it’s quite hard to choose just one. My favorite for shooting is Stockholm; I love how the stations are nestled deep underground in the rock, and each one is differently colored. Every system has plenty of great architects, stations, and details. But I will always have a special place in my heart for two metro systems: Prague and Berlin. They are the best for me in terms of experiences related to shooting not just metro architecture but also more controversial themes like illegal tunnel exploration or photographing guys painting graffiti on the subways (shhh!).

Last year, I published a photo zine on this topic called “Chapter Closed”. I’ve visited Berlin about 30 times in the last five years, and it never ceases to amaze me with the differences in the metro environment and the experiences associated with them. I will always hold Prague in my heart; if I had to choose just one system, it will always be Prague.

© @Dami1992 \| Film: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

What’s next on the horizon for you? Are there any upcoming projects you’re excited to explore next?

I’m currently working on several long-term projects; I want to create a book about subway systems and their architecture, which will be completely shot on film, of course. I’m also preparing material for a smaller zine from the housing estate where I grew up and still spend time, where I’m documenting the place around me on film, whether it’s concrete architecture or people and their interactions in this environment. I have a lot of other film projects already started, and I’m beginning to work on them, so there’s definitely a lot to look forward to!

© @Dami1992 \| Film: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

If you would like to check out other photos from David, make sure to follow him on Instagram!

With every new addition to the Lomography lineup comes the same irresistible question: what will the first rolls reveal? The Lomography Manila team recently put the new Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera to test and returned with first impressions, favorite frames, and new discoveries.

What excited you most about trying the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera for the first time?

Janelle: I found the camera's feel to be fascinating, and once I had it in my hands, it was simple to understand. Because of its simplicity and the fact that I could take twice as many images, I was able to be more creative and carefree without worrying about running out of shots. It was intriguing to try to come up with more and more ways to compose shots to fill the entire roll.

Credits: @denise, @sylvann, @nate\_soriano, @jhondaniel, @janelle-jose, & @francinegaebriele \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

Nate: One of the things I was looking forward to was seeing how the camera would stand up against other Lomography cameras – specifically the standard Simple Use Reloadable Cameras and the Half-frame Lomourette. The Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera is the perfect cross between these two products, but packaged into a more compact and portable format.

Denise: As a slow shooter, I’m usually not a big fan of half-frame cameras because it takes me forever to finish a roll. Ironically, that’s exactly what excited me most about trying the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera. Since we were also working with a time constraint, it felt like a challenge to see if we could actually practice the Lomographic way of shooting: “Don’t think, just shoot.”

Could you share your first adventures with the camera? Where did it take you, and what moments ended up in your first roll?

Jhon: The team and I first took photos inside the office, taking indoor portraits that were made more fun because of the color gels. Afterwards, we went outside to just experiment and play around our usual surroundings. Our roll ended up with portraits of random scenarios like car mirror selfies, using the telephone as props, etc.

AJ: What I liked the most about my first time with the camera was how we ended up embracing the parking lot aesthetic for it – being creative in a limiting environment, the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera being a fitting format for the overall electric vibe that we had during the shoot, and everyone pitching in ideas.

Credits: @denise, @sylvann, @nate\_soriano, @jhondaniel, @janelle-jose, & @francinegaebriele \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

When you finally got the results back, how did the photos compare to what you had imagined?

Nate: It blew my expectations! Despite being as straightforward and simple as it is, the photos were quite crisp with a certain 90s to early 2000s charm.

Jhon: It turned out great, and I really love how the color translated! It’s always exciting to see whether I have captured the correct frame to make the perfect diptych, but that’s the beauty of the half-frame format – sometimes, what I don't envision turns out to be more interesting!

What did the combination of the camera and the LomoChrome Classicolor bring to your photos?

Denise: Lots of reds and vibrant colors, especially since most of the photos were taken outdoors during the afternoon. The film really amplified the energy of the team and made everything feel a little livelier.

Janelle: It gave a more fun and youthful feel to the photos. The results feel bright and have a certain pop to it.

AJ: I think it highlighted the summer sun that afternoon. We also had pops of color in a lot of the frames, and it brought out that contrast of color against the half-empty parking lot.

Credits: @denise, @sylvann, @nate\_soriano, @jhondaniel, @janelle-jose, & @francinegaebriele \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

What was it like shooting with the team and seeing everyone add their own perspectives? Any memorable behind-the-scenes moments?

Denise: The most memorable part is probably how we constantly try to make the most out of our very limited setting: the office and the office parking lot. Sometimes we think our location is going to make the photos look boring, but with some good direction and a willingness to have fun, we end up producing great photos. It’s a good reminder that you don’t really need an elaborate setup to shoot something interesting.

AJ: One memorable moment was when we asked the security guard if we could borrow some chairs for the shoot. I think the guards here have come to know us as the young people who pet the cats and shoot film cameras outside. He was so supportive and let us take as many chairs as we wanted.

Credits: @denise, @sylvann, @nate\_soriano, @jhondaniel, @janelle-jose, & @francinegaebriele \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

Nate: It was a crazy fun experience! You could really see a piece of everyone’s personality imbued into the way they took their shots or posed for photographs. Some memorable moments that come to mind are the times we had to get creative with the compositions (since we worked in a pretty small area), so we climbed roofs, ran across the parking lot, laid down on office desks, etc.

Tell us how these playful diptychs came about. How did the team work together to create them?

AJ: Lots of talking and laughing! At first, we looked for pegs for poses on the internet, but at some point, everyone just started playing around with the environment, collaborating and letting our whims take us wherever. It was like hanging out with friends, and we just happened to have a camera to document it with.

Jhon: Everyone took turns to capture from different angles. Having different perspectives really made the playful diptychs come to life!

Janelle: Most of the shots were quite impulsive and everyone was encouraged to just throw everything out and see what sticks.

Credits: @denise, @sylvann, @nate\_soriano, @jhondaniel, @janelle-jose, & @francinegaebriele \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

Denise: The Lomo Manila team is a playful and creative bunch. When we received the prototype unit, we were excited to shoot just about anything with it. After finishing our main tasks for the day, we headed outside the office and started coming up with random concepts on the spot. While we intentionally planned a few diptychs, the entire shoot was still very spontaneous. I think the time constraint also pushed us to come up with some clutch, fun ideas that ended up looking unexpectedly cool.

Was there a frame from the roll that instantly stood out to you when you saw the results?

AJ: Many frames stood out to me, but I like the shot of us on the rooftop the most. That rooftop directly connected to our office window has been a go-to spot for Lomo employees since we moved here. Sunlight's great there during the afternoon, and the photos always end up looking like scenes from a coming-of-age movie. Looking at that photo makes me think of how much I really enjoy being around these people.

Janelle: The shot that stood for me was the one where all of us were sitting on the rooftop. It really captured a devil-may-care vibe.

Credits: @denise, @sylvann, @nate\_soriano, @jhondaniel, @janelle-jose, & @francinegaebriele \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

Jhon: The car mirror selfie instantly caught my eye! It turned out even better than I imagined – the playful distortion made it even more interesting. Together with the running shot, it really just set the mood for the entire frame!

Nate: Definitely the photos of the team posed like something out of an album cover – courtesy of @francinegaebriele. I think it showcased how the Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera also has the capacity for more serious projects or compositions apart from capturing organic and wacky moments.

Denise: The “band photo,” except we’re not actually a band. Nate’s red shirt worked incredibly well with the Classicolor, and Gabe did a great job directing the pose. It ended up looking way cooler than any of us expected!

Credits: @denise, @sylvann, @nate\_soriano, @jhondaniel, @janelle-jose, & @francinegaebriele \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

Where do you see yourself taking the camera next?

Jhon: Definitely when I travel again, and I think the next one's a beach trip! Honestly, the camera is so portable that it's really accessible to just bring around. I could see myself reaching for this camera all the time.

Denise: I’ve mentioned this in another article before, but I love traveling, and bringing a film camera has always been one of my travel essentials. The Lomo MC-A is perfect when I want more deliberate and composed shots, but if I want to have fun and not worry about running out of frames or immediately reloading another roll, I’d definitely bring the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera instead.

Nate: On top of my head, probably to a gig at night. I think it’d be a good chance to test out the flash and gel filters!

AJ: Somewhere with lots of people and interesting things to see, like a book market or a gig!

Janelle: I see the camera as something I can bring anywhere, given its size. It’s also the type of camera I can share with friends to use in any sort of occasion, encouraging them to capture memories with me.

On May 15, eight participants set off from Jing'an Temple in Shanghai, each armed with a Lomo MC-A and a roll of LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200. They headed east along Fumin Road, Julu Road, and Changle Road – a three-street stretch that became their color-hunting playground.

Photo by Yin Hang with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

Each participant was assigned a color to chase but nothing else was prescribed. No fixed subjects, no must-shoot spots. A faded retro red on a brick wall, a dusty blue outside a café, the warm amber glow of sunlit leaves overhead; the city already holds countless hues. This time, they simply chose to focus on one.

Now, let’s look back on the LomoWalk through the eyes of two participants: Xiongzai and Tang Xiawen.

Photo by Zhou Yijia and Ding Gishen with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

Xiongzai & The Blue

Photo by Xiongzai with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

Before setting out, Xiongzai had a romantic vision in mind: the pale blue of old villa walls beneath plane trees and chic storefront displays, the denim blue on stylish passersby in the streets. She even imagined stumbling upon something unexpected – a moment, a person, a story that made the hunt worthwhile.

But half an hour into walking along Fumin Road and Julu Road, she still hadn't captured a single frame of blue. The only blues she kept running into were blue signboards, blue tarps covering scaffolding, scattered blue shared bikes. At that moment, she couldn't help but wonder, is the color blue in this city only for construction and maintenance?

“I felt a bit frustrated, honestly. I started taking photos of those ‘ugly blues’ with my phone instead, saving the camera for what I actually wanted to shoot.” So she turned her lens toward things that weren't blue but felt more worth capturing: weathered walls, dappled shadows of leaves, a lazy cat at the entrance of an alleyway.

After the official walk ended, she continued along Wuyuan Road and Anfu Road, finally gathering bits of blue from gallery artworks and more shop displays. Her conclusion: “Finding blue in the city is really, really hard.” And yet, it didn't disappoint her. It made her think, and start asking: where exactly does blue live in this city?

Photo by Xiongzai with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

“The beauty of the MC-A is that it can be as casual or as deliberate as you want it to be. It's lightweight, the metal body feels great in hand, and it looks good, too. Function-wise, you can rely entirely on auto mode and just press the shutter, or you can manually adjust focus distance, shutter speed, timer, and even go manual focus.” She specifically mentioned the multiple exposure feature, which makes shooting double exposures incredibly easy.

She also gave the splitzer a try and shot a four-frame grid. “The first frame was misaligned (laughs), and the final image didn't quite match what I saw through the viewfinder, it ended up more centered.” She experimented with multiple exposures, too, “but maybe the subjects weren't the right fit – the results lacked that ‘artistic’ feel.”

Photo by Xiongzai with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

Don't Think? This Might Be the Golden Rule for P-people

Among Lomography's classic 10 Golden Rules, the one that stands out most is: Don't Think, Just Shoot. After this LomoWalk, Xiongzai seems to have started embracing that spontaneous philosophy.

“Honestly, the Golden Rules sound like they were written for P-people \[referring to the MBTI system\] – haha,” she laughed.

When asked if she captured any “magic shots,” she admitted she didn't stumble upon anything spectacular. “The event was only a few hours long, after all – those magic moments are rare.” But she did capture something else: a lazy summer vibe. The photos don't tell dramatic stories, they carry that relaxed, unhurried feel of a quiet afternoon.

Still, there was one photo she couldn't help mentioning. “I saw a girl walking her dog. The building behind her had such clean colors, and there was a tree I really loved in the foreground. But when I raised my camera, she had already walked behind the tree. Luckily, she stepped back out.”

When she got the final image, it looked different from what she'd imagined: “The girl looked a bit rushed in the shot, and there was a delivery rider speeding past. Not exactly the relaxed, warm feeling I had in mind.” But then she paused. Maybe that's the Lomo spirit? “Embracing the unexpected – that's part of the fun, isn't it?”

Photo by Xiongzai with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

Her Pick: Two Blues, and the Story Lies in Their Rarity

Photo by Xiongzai with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

When asked, “If you had to choose one photo from this LomoWalk as your ‘color’ representative, which one would it be?”, Xiongzai hesitated a little. “Blue? I barely captured any blue on camera.”

In the end, she chose a double exposure. The first shot was of a man holding a blue-and-white porcelain cup. Right after that, she spotted a blue mirror in a jewelry store, and lined up the second exposure. “The composition wasn't quite right,” she admitted. “It didn't fully capture the story of that rare moment – encountering two blues, one right after the other.”

Xiawen & The Yellow

Unlike Xiong Zai, Tang Xiawen seemed to be “favored” from the very beginning of the game.

Photo by Tang Xiawen with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

She drew yellow. “At first, I wasn't thinking of a bright, vibrant yellow, more the kind that feels like old film in a Shanghai summer: the glare off a taxi windshield, the faded warmth of an old residential wall baking in the sun.”

“Even before we started, I felt this route was perfect for capturing that laid-back city vibe. The stretch from Jing'an Temple to Julu Road has this unmistakably mixed character – plane trees, old villas, cafés, cyclists, and those small, fleeting moments that feel accidental.” And yellow kept appearing in her frame, almost without her looking for it. “I didn't really plan what to shoot. I was more like waiting for yellow to show up on its own.” And it did.

Photo by Tang Xiawen with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

Chance, Wandering, Summer: Her Three Words for the Day

“Chance, wandering, summer.” Tang Xiawen summed up the day in three words. “Along this route, you never really get stuck asking yourself ‘what should I shoot?’ Instead, you're constantly drawn in by the light, the colors, the people passing by. Most of the photos came from those fleeting moments, just right place, right time.”

And that unpredictability is exactly what makes film photography so compelling. When you can't instantly check what you've just captured, your attention shifts back to the moment itself – the light, the scene, the color that made you stop in the first place.

Photo by Tang Xiawen with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

She Captured More Than Just Color

Tang Xiawen was especially drawn to the tones of LomoChrome Classicolor. “It really brings out that warm, cozy atmosphere of Shanghai's streets—especially the yellows and reds. There's an almost oily, film-like richness to them.”

In that kind of light, she stopped worrying about whether her shots were “finished.” What mattered was the moment that made her press the shutter. “One moment that really stuck with me: I just casually shot a piece of glass lit up by sunlight, but because of the color shifts from the filter and the film itself, the final image came out almost dreamlike. It hit me then – film doesn't just record what's real. It can hold emotion and memory, too.”

“Most of the time, I don't start with a concept. I just tune into the city and let the pictures happen.”

Photo by Tang Xiawen with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

Her Pick: No Need to Look for It – It Was Already There

Photo by Tang Xiawen with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

When asked to choose one photo from the LomoWalk as her “color” representative, Tang Xiawen didn't hesitate.

“I'd pick this one as my ‘yellow’.”

In the frame, an elderly woman in yellow is holding the man’s arm next to her as they walk slowly forward. The afternoon sun falls softly across her back, washing the whole scene in a quiet warmth. “Shanghai streets are usually so fast and crowded,” she said, “but in that moment, everything suddenly felt still.”

For her, that's exactly what makes Lomo photography special. “Most of the time, you can't fully predict how the shot will turn out. But what ends up staying with you is often the truest feeling of that moment.”

Photo by Jia Jingxian,Yin Hang and Wo Jihong with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

In two hours, the walk didn't uncover every shade, but it did uncover a new way of looking. The real takeaway wasn't what they shot; it was what they finally noticed.

Photo by Zhou Yijia and Yin Hang with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

Thank you to everyone who joined us for a walk, a chat, and a few rolls of film on that early summer afternoon. Your perspectives turned an ordinary stretch of street into something worth documenting, one frame at a time.

Looking forward to crossing paths again – through the lens.

Photo by Tang Xiawen with Lomo MC-A 35 mm Film Camera and LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

We invited illustrator Nicole Tecchio to slow down and share her story through a series of instant photographs taken with the Lomo’Instant Automat Glass. The result is Casa Vacanze (“Holiday Home”), a visual diary that intertwines memories, imagination, and everyday objects to bring a personal narrative to life, moving between analogue photography and illustration.

In this interview, Nicole talks about the creative process behind the project and reflects on the meaning of creativity when using an archive of objects, images, and details from everyday life. She also explains how using an instant camera introduced a new dimension of spontaneity to her work, encouraging her to experiment and embrace unpredictable results.

© Nicole Tecchio with the Soft Cover Album & Lomo’Instant Automat Glass

Hi, Nicole! Welcome to Lomography Magazine! Could you please briefly introduce yourself to our readers?

Hi, everyone! I’m Nicole Tecchio, an illustrator and librarian. I mainly work as an illustrator in the publishing industry, but I'm fascinated by the world of visual art in general, especially photography, which I often combine with drawing.

© Nicole Tecchio with the Soft Cover Album & Lomo’Instant Automat Glass

How do you typically collect and store ideas, inspiration, and moments from your daily life?

I have a deep passion for collecting, especially when it comes to flyers, business cards, postcards, and photographs. I rely heavily on my personal image archive, which I’m constantly updating. I need to be completely immersed in images in order to work, which is why I have a series of bulletin boards where I pin the images that strike me the most, and I rearrange them three or four times a year.

© Nicole Tecchio with the Soft Cover Album & Lomo’Instant Automat Glass

Tell us how you came up with the idea for “Casa Vacanze”, and how this project brought together your work as an illustrator and your passion for analogue photography.

Casa Vacanze is a project in which I chose to have fun first and foremost. I’m very attached to the family aspect of photography, personal memories, and small home archives. That's definitely the realm where I feel most at home when working with photography. I place great importance on constructing a narrative arc with a healthy dose of irony, and whenever possible, mixing different media and creating a dialogue between them. Casa Vacanze naturally brought all these aspects together. It’s a private collection of images within a strong relational context. The images could suggest a narrative while also being playful and imaginative.

© Nicole Tecchio with the Soft Cover Album & Lomo’Instant Automat Glass

Has instant photography changed the way you tell stories, capture memories, and document everyday life?

I find the limitations of instant photography (imperfection and spontaneity) inspiring. As designers, we're accustomed to planning images, layouts, compositions, shadows, and lighting with great precision. Having a limited number of shots and not being able to edit photos precisely forces us to take a leap of faith and embrace the beauty of results that are, in some ways, beyond our control.

© Nicole Tecchio with the Soft Cover Album & Lomo’Instant Automat Glass

Do you have a favorite page or picture? If so, why?

That’s a tough choice! I’d probably choose the postcard featuring the “Sleeping Beauty” set. I love fairy tales and enjoy bringing them into the present day. Once developed, the snapshot surprised me a great deal; the result was different from what I’d imagined, far exceeding my expectations.

© Nicole Tecchio with the Soft Cover Album & Lomo’Instant Automat Glass

In Casa Vacanze, Nicole transforms instant photography into a space for memories, play, and storytelling. It's a personal diary that encourages us to slow down, observe, and find inspiration in life's little moments.

Thank you, Nicole, for inviting us into your Analogue Journal! To stay updated on her work, be sure to follow her on Instagram.

Lomography has partners all over the world to help serve the Community's analogue needs. Today, we are joined by Simon Hepburn from UK-based Share Your Story, who tells us about the roots of the photography store and venue, as well as plans geared towards expanding its analogue community.

Credits: Share Your Story

Store Information

Name: Share Your Story

Location: Altrincham, Greater Manchester, UK

Film Services: All film development and scanning offsite, Printing to A1 onsite

Website/Social Media: shareyourstory.uk \| Instagram: @ share\your\story\_uk / TikTok: @ shareyourstoryuk / LinkedIn: @ shareyourstoryuk

Available in Store: Lomography films and cameras

Hi, and welcome to Lomography Magazine! What’s the story behind Share Your Story? How did it all start?

I had a number of different jobs in marketing and teaching and came to the realization that people so often miss the chance to capture and share the important things in their lives – whether that’s as simple as doing something with holiday photographs, capturing their life stories in a memoir, or just sharing what their businesses or charities do well. Initial market research also showed that huge numbers of people buy cameras or start to write a novel but don’t have the time, the confidence, or the skills to follow through on these.

Share Your Story was started in response – as well as selling creative equipment, we also offer advice, run clubs and training courses, have our own studio for content creation and offer a range of services including media transfer, printing, and film development. We also hold competitions and exhibitions to inspire people on their creative journey. Our goal is to remove as many barriers as possible to storytelling!

Credits: Share Your Story

What is your favorite part about running Share Your Story?

Talking to people who come into the store. So many conversations start with the customer saying ‘so what exactly do you do, then?’ and this leads to many directions with many solutions. People tell us it’s a very different experience to most shops!

In your opinion, what role does analogue photography play in our current times?

When we started learning about Lomography, we came across your slogan – “An imperfect solution for a perfect world”. That really sums up our experience, with people turning to film to get away from the instant, glossed-up and AI’d world of phone photography or pixel-peeping with top-end mirrorless cameras. Our customers are often looking for a camera that they don’t mind handing around to friends, or will produce pictures that just look different!

Credits: Share Your Story

What is the film photography community like in Share Your Story these days? Do you think there are more young people getting into film?

We’ve been hugely surprised by the interest in film photography in Altrincham since we opened. We now sell over 15 types of film. Our film club has over 80 members aged from 17 to well over 70, with experience ranging from absolute beginners to people with decades of experience. Interestingly, the people who run our film club (Sam) and introductory film course (Ed) are both in their early 20s.

Credits: Share Your Story

Do you have a favorite Lomography product, or one you often recommend to your customers?

We’re always recommending the Simple Use Reloadable Cameras. We do sell a lot of disposable cameras but they’re not as environmentally friendly as they could be; the Simple Use ones are great for those trying out film, and we like Lomography’s fun approach to photography with the filters on the flash.

Credits: Share Your Story

Lastly, do you have any future plans for the store, or projects you’re working on, that you can tell us about?

We’ve just finished soundproofing our studio, so we’re now really excited about the potential of using it for podcasting, audiobooks, and much more. One of our staff is an audio engineer and we use (and sell) Røde equipment so we’re ready to create high quality audio to back up photography. We’re also in the process of launching ‘Culture Club’ – a regular meeting of creatives from all disciplines from the local area.

To keep up to date with everything from Share Your Story in the UK, follow them on their Instagram and check out their website. Check out other Lomography Partners through the Store Locator.

UK-based videographer and director Jason Osayamen is currently working on his debut feature film, a psychological thriller set in Nigeria titled “Pre Death Do Us Part”. The protagonist of the film is a man who embarks on a peculiar journey to uncover the true identity of his fiancée, only to find himself tangled in a web of dark secrets. Jason chose to use the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens for several scenes and talked to us about using alternative lenses to add visual depth to his cinematography.

Welcome to the Magazine, Jason! Could you give us a quick introduction about yourself?

My name is Jason Osayamen, and I’m a filmmaker, writer, director, and producer. I’m the founder of Vintage Screen Media and currently working on my debut feature film, “Pre Death Do Us Part”, a psychological thriller that explores love, perception, and hidden truths.

My work is heavily influenced by visual storytelling, atmosphere, and the emotional connection between the audience and the image. I’m always interested in experimenting with tools that can bring character and personality to a frame.

Tell us about your time with the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Art Lens. Where did you take it, and what did you end up shooting?

Shortly after the script was completed, we began looking for a lens with a distinct character that would complement the visual language I had envisioned for the film. We were fortunate to get our hands on this lens and immediately started testing it in a variety of scenarios before bringing it into production. So far, we have used it across a range of environments, including interior scenes, outdoor locations, and controlled lighting setups.

It has been particularly useful for character-driven moments, environmental details, and scenes where mood and atmosphere are essential. The lens has allowed us to explore different visual textures while maintaining a strong narrative focus.

Still from “Pre Death Do Us Part” by Jason Osayamen, using the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

What were your first impressions? How would you describe its personality?

My first impression was that the lens had a very distinctive character. It didn't feel overly clinical or sterile; rather, it brought a sense of emotion and personality to the image. I would describe it as expressive, cinematic, and artistic.

It has a look that encourages creativity and makes you think more carefully about composition and depth rather than simply chasing technical perfection. The images felt organic and visually engaging straight out of the camera.

Credits: Jason Osayamen

Were there any particular moments – certain lighting setups or subjects – where the lens really came alive for you?

The lens really came alive during scenes with practical lighting and strong subject separation. Low-light environments and scenes with background highlights allowed its character to shine through. We particularly enjoyed using it during emotionally intimate moments between characters because the rendering helped draw attention directly to the subject while maintaining a beautiful sense of depth. It also performed wonderfully during golden hour, where the transition between focused and out-of-focus areas created a very cinematic atmosphere.

Still from “Pre Death Do Us Part” by Jason Osayamen, using the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

From setup to wrap, how did the lens work with your camera setup? Did features like the adjustable bokeh levels, focus coupling, or follow focus compatibility affect the way you framed a shot?

Although production is still ongoing, the lens has integrated smoothly into our workflow and worked exceptionally well with our camera setup. Features such as the adjustable bokeh settings have provided valuable creative flexibility, allowing us to adapt the visual style depending on the mood of a scene. The focus mechanism feels reliable, and its compatibility with follow focus systems has been especially useful during more controlled cinematic shots. Overall, it has been a practical tool that complements both the technical and creative demands of the production.

Still from “Pre Death Do Us Part” by Jason Osayamen, using the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

How did the bokeh character influence the mood or style of your shots?

The bokeh has played a significant role in shaping the emotional tone of the images we've captured so far. It helps separate the characters from their surroundings while still preserving a strong sense of atmosphere within the frame. Since “Pre Death Do Us Part” is a psychological thriller, visual mood is essential to the storytelling, and the lens has allowed us to introduce a subtle dreamlike quality without distracting from the narrative.

Depending on the scene, the bokeh can feel romantic, mysterious, or even slightly unsettling, adding an extra emotional layer to the imagery. Rather than simply serving as a visual effect, it has become an important storytelling tool that helps reinforce the tone and psychology of each moment.

Still from “Pre Death Do Us Part” by Jason Osayamen, using the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

Any tips you'd share with someone curious to try this lens?

My biggest advice would be to embrace the lens's character rather than trying to make it behave like a conventional modern lens. Experiment with different lighting conditions, shoot wide open when appropriate, and pay attention to how backgrounds interact with your subject. Take time to understand how the lens responds to practical lights, reflections, and depth. The more you work with it, the more you'll discover unique creative opportunities. It's a lens that rewards experimentation and can help filmmakers develop a more distinctive visual style.
